# PROTOCOL ANALYSIS: Verbal Reports as Data K.
Anders Ericsson and Herbert A.
Simon Although psychologists have often employed the technigue of protocol analysis—or the use of the subject's own verbal reports as data—in exploring cognitive processes, the technique's nature and reliability have been poorly understood.
This book finally puts protocol analysis on firm ground by examining its underlying assumptions, techniques, and limitations.
It adresses such key questions as what sorts of mental events are reliable; what the role of the investigator's interpretations should be in helping to understand such data; and what mental events cannot be explained by protocols.
The authors describe a general theory of cognitive processes and structure, which, they argue, accounts for verbalization and verbal reports.
The theory is presented in the form of an information processing modei.
Major issues surrounding the use and validity of verbal reports are taken up and empirical studies are discussed within the framework of the model.
The book focuses on reports of cognitive processes, but the concepts and models it employs can be extended to such areas of verbal behavior as psychophysics, survey design, and measurement of personality traits.

In the limiting case, we would like to have process models so explicit that they could actually produce the predicted behavior from the information in the stimulus.
This concern for the course of the cognitive processes has revived intercst in finding ways to incrcasc the temporal density of observations so as to reveal intermediate stages of thc processes.
Increasingly, investigators record the directions of the subject's gaze (eye movements), and thc intermediate bchaviors (movements or physical manipulations of stimulus material) that precede the solution or criterion performance.
Since data on intermediate processing are costly to gather and analyze, it is important to consider carefully how such data can be interprcted validly, and what contribution they can make to our undcrstanding of the phenomena under study.
One means frequently used to gain information about the course of the cognitive proccsses is to probe the subjects' internal states by verbal methods.
'These methods are the topic of this monograph.

About Verbal Data Since the triumph of bchaviorism over "introspcctively" oricnted compcting vicwpoints, verbal rcports have bccn suspcct as data.

## Extracting
Data from Behavior The notion that verbal reports provide possibly interesting but only informal information, to be verified by other data, has affected the ways in which verbalizations are collected and analyzed.
If the purpose of obtaining verbal reports is mainly to gencrate hypotheses and ideas, investigators need not concern themsclves (and generally have not concerned themsclves) with methodological questions about data collection.
As a result, there is litle publishcd litcrature on such issucs, thc datagathering and data-analysis mcthods actually uscd vary tremcndously, and thc details of these methods arc reportcd skctchily in rescarch publications that make use of such data.
If we are to make rapid and continuing progrcss in understanding human cognitive processcs, this state of affairs is wholly unsatisfactory.
In the first place, no clear guidclincs are providcd to distinguish illegitimate "introspection" from the many forms of verbal output that are routinely treated as data-as passing the chain and transit test (see the cxamples above).
On what thcoretical or practical grounds do we distinguish bctwecn the subject's "yes" or "no" in a concept attainment experimcnt and his assertion that the hypothesis he is entertaining is "small ycilow circle"?
In the second place, no distinctions are made among such diverse forms of verbalization as thinking-aloud (TΛ) protocols, retrospective responses to specific probes, and the classical introspcctive reports of trained observers.
All are jointly and loosely condemned as "introspection."

## Soft
versus Hard Data Somc investigators call verbal reports and verbal descriptions "soft data" in contrast to simple bchavioral measures like latency or corrcctness of response, which are rcferred to as "hard." What docs this distinction mcan?
In scicncc one would like to maintain as clcar a separation as possible between data and theory.
Data are supposed to derivc directly from obscrvation; theories are supposcd to account for, cxplain, and prcdict these observation-based data. lata arc "hard" whcn there is intersubjective agrcemcnt that they corrcspond to thc facts of the obscrved behavior.
Even psychoanalytically or existentially oriented psychologists will accept response latencies as data—even though being possibly irrelevant data for cxplaining bchavior.
When, however, an analyst codes a fivesecond description of a dream as "oral fixation," many psychologists would argue that this encoding is not a datum but a subjective interprctation of the data (i.e., of the verbal description of the dream).
Surely, theory-laden inferences were required to dcrive the encoding from the verbal protocol.
Data are regarded as "soft" to the degree that they incorporatc such inferences, especially when the theoretical premises and rules of inference are themselves not completely explicit and objective.
'The problem with "soft" data is that different intcrprcters making different inferences will not agree in their encodings, and cach interpreter is likely, wittingly or not, to arrive at an interpretation that is favorable to his thcoretical orientation.
The hard-soft distinction is orthogonal to the distinction between verbal and non-verbal.
'The same problems of inference can cmerge in observers' attempts to understand non-verbal events (c.g., sequences of physical movements, pieces of ımusic).
Such events may require as much interpretation as is required to understand verbal sequences.
Technological advances have enhanced our ability to trcat verbal protocols as hard data.
Until tape recorders were gencrally available, it was common practice for experimenters to take selective notes of verbalizations, paraphrasing and omitting whatever was "unimportant." In analyzing such notes further, it was impossible to distinguish the inferences from the original verbalizations.
Using encodings of verbal protocols as data has often been made cven more difficult because the thcorics cmployed, explicitly or implicitly, in thc encoding were formulated in very general terms.
'The search for general mcchanisms also led to overall interpretations of entire protocols with little concern for encoding and explicating individual protocol statements.
More recent research based on explicit information processing models of the cognitive proccsses has causcd thinking-aloud verbalizations to be viewed in a ncw light.
It is now standard proccdure to make carcful verbatim transcripts of the recorded tapes, thus prescrving the raw data in as "hard" a form as could bc wished. Λt the same time, information processing models of the cognitive processes provide a basis for making the encoding process cxplicit and objcctivc, so that the theorctical presuppositions cntering into that process can be examined objcctively.

## Theoretical
Presupposition in Encoding Clyde Coombs, in his book A Theory of Data, shows that raw data go through a typical sequence of steps on the route from initial obscrvation to the edited and encodcd form in which they are used to test thcories or make prcdictions.
'T'hese steps, which are not neutral with respcct to theory, can be secn in the processing of protocol data as they can with other kinds of data.
At the first step, theory delimits a small portion of the universe of potentially obscrvable behavior as being relevant.
'This judgment of relevance determines what behaviors should be recorded.
At the next step, thesc behaviors are cncoded in a manncr that is again determined on thcoretical grounds.
In thc case of verbal behavior, the proccss bcgins with a taperecording, containing essentially all thc auditory cvents that occurred during the cxperimental session. ln producing from the tape a written transcript, somc selection is required.
After the temporal information, repetitions, and stress have been uscd to segment and parse the verbal stream, most of this information is usually eliminated from the transcript, except as it is captured by punctuation.
We will refer to this transcription step as preprocessing.
At the next step, the preprocessed scgments are cncoded into the terminology of the theoretical model.
'This is oftcn achicved by first detcrmining coding categories, a priori, and then having human judges make the coding assessments.
If each of the segments is to be treated as an independent datum, thcn the encoding of that scgment must be made on thc basis of the information contained in it, independently of the surrounding scgments.
In Chaptcr 6 of this book, wc will discuss at some length mcthods for carrying out this kind of local encoding, and the conditions that must be met to make it possible.
Verbal protocols have bcen analyzed in two rathcr different ways.
One method claims not to require the analysis of meanings, while the other docs rcquire it.
In the first kind of analysis, subject and experimenter have agreed, by prior instruction, upon spccific signals, which may be spccch signals or button presses, for their communication.
These signals are mostly arbitrary— a subject could say "cef' instcad of "yes"; communication is possible only because of thc agrccmcnt cstablished between subject and experiincnter.
'To analyzc the recorded verbalizations under these conditions, the experimenter has only to catcgorize each speech signal into one of the agrccd-upon categorics.
In theory, if not in practice, a codcr should not even need to know the subject's language—assuring that no mcaningful analysis or inferencing is involved.
A large number of paradigms in psychology use this kind of analysis.
For cxample, studies using scales and multiple-choice alternatives can all be scen as instances of this method.
In the sccond kind of analysis, thc obscrved vcrbalizations are analyzed in terms of thcir mcanings.
Even in this casc, the thcory guiding the analysis limits the encoding to selccted aspects and features rather than thc full mcaning of the verbalization.
For example, in a typical concept attainment task, cach instancc or stimulus can be represented as a uniquc combination of fcatures.
Fach distinct conccpt can be represented by some particular configuration of fcatures.

Although the space of logically possible different conccpts may be very large, it is severely limited comparcd with thc variability of natural languagc.
'l’hus a verbalization like "red circles are cefs" can normally bc cncoded as identical with "blood-colored round ones are cef's." T'he context of a particular theory and cxperiment greatly constrains the range of possible interprctation and allows thc meaningful analysis of verbalizations to be selcctive and incompletc.

I'll just guess on this onc." Many examples can be cited of this kind of mcaningful analysis, where verbalizations are mapped onto a priori formal alternatives.
'T’he analysis of memory for mcaningful text has been studicd by Kintsch (1974) and many others.
Newell and Simon (1972) analyzed tasks, idcntifying formally defined knowledge states in terms of which subjccts thinking-aloud protocols could be encoded.
Many analyses of verbalizations do not fit thc above scheme, including most analyses that scck to arrivc at an undcrstanding of the verbalizations.

## Inferring
Thought Processes From Behavior It is sometimes believed that using verbal data implies accepting the subjects' interpretation of them or of thc cvents that are reported.
This issue of trust has its origins in our everyday experiencc and use of language.
In order to communicatc effectively with other pcople, wc accept their word for many facts.

Subjects'reports of their own mental states and mental processes raisc slightly different issues of trust.
According to a naive theory of consciousness, subjects have the sole direct access to thcir own mental states and processes.
'Thc subjective fceling of onc's ability to report one's own mental experiences veridically is strong.
For a great many reasons, this confidence is not shared by experimental psychologists, who have shown that under numcrous circumstances such sclf-reports are unreliable.
However, the issuc of thc reliability of self-reports can (and, we think, should) be avoidcd entirely.
Thc report "X" nccd not be used to infer that X is truc, but only that thc subject was able to say "X"—(i.e., had the information that cnabled him to say "X.") Then Stockholm popped up and I remembered that is where the Nobel prizes are awarded: then I felt sure I could answer "yes." In the first case we have to trust the subject if we want to infer that he actually knows the capital, whcrcas in the third case it is unlikcly that hc could gcncratc the correct namc unless it werc acccssible from memory.

## Some
Basic Assumptions We can now summarize the basic assumptions that set the stage for our further cxplorations.
Most fundamentally, we sec verbal bchavior as one type of recordable behavior, which should be observed and analyzed like any other behavior.
'Thc cognitive processes that generate verbalizations are a subset of the cognitive processes that gencratc any kind of recordable response or behavior.
Hence, we would look for the same kind of "mechanical" and complete process description of verbal bchavior as of other kinds of behavior, and we would not acccpt magical or privilcged processes as explanations for verbalizations.
Whether one can and should trust subjccts' verbal reports is not a matter of faith but an empirical issue on a par with the issue of validating other types of bchavior, like eye fixations or motor behavior.
A single invalid verbal report should not force us to discard analysis of verbal reports generally.
Indecd, this monograph will undcrtake to build a theory of verbalization, so that we can thcn specify whcn, where, and under what kinds of instructions informative verbal reports can be obtained from subjects.
Postulating that the cognitive processes underlying verbalization are a subset of all cognitive processes implies that verbalization must comply with thc constraints that have bcen identified, cxpcrimentally, to govern all cognitive processes.
'These information processing constraints will provide powerful guidelines for our attempts to specify how observed verbalizations could have been gencratcd.
We wish to account for verbally reported information by proposing a proccssing model sufficicntly powerful to regenerate that information.

## Plan
of Attack Our first task is to describe a gencral thcory of cognitive processes and structurc, which, wc argue, accounts for verbalizations and verbal reports.
For rcasons that have alrcady been statcd, thc analysis must be carricd out within a framework of theory.
T'his framcwork must be sufficiently general to permit us to relate, within a unified perspective, all thc kinds of data that arc commonly used in psychological cxperiments.
Usually, in choosing bctwecn theories, we want to pick the strongest one—thc one that will make the strongest predictions.
In the present case, where the theory we choose will influence the way in which wc encode and analyze our data, wc want to pick the weakcst and most "neutral" one that can do the job.
'The fewer controversial assumptions wc incorporate in the theory, the less we will bc involved in the circularity of using theory-laden data to test our theorics.
Nevertheless, there appears to be no way of processing data that does not incorporate some thcorctical assumptions about the systcm and proccsses that gcneratcd the data.
Our particular stratcgy will be to set forth the theory in its most gencral, hence lcast controversial, form first, then add more specific hypotheses where they are required.
After presenting the theory as an information processing model of cognitive processes, we will survey the literature on verbal reporting and derive from it a taxonomy of reporting procedures.
We will follow this survey with an historical review of carlier approaches to verbal reports.
We will then take up the major issues surrounding the use and validity of verbal reports, discussing the cmpirical studics within thc framcwork of a more detailed information processing model.

## THE
PROCESSING MODEL Our purpose in presenting a spccific processing model is to aid us in intcrpreting verbal data obtaincd from subjects and the relation of their verbal to thcir other behavior.
Since the data (including the verbal data) arc gathered in order to tcst thcorics about thc human information proccssing system, we are cngaged in something of a bootstrap operation.
We need a model in order to interpret data that are to be used, in turn, to test the model.
Under these circumstances, our data-interpretation model should be as simple as possible, and it must not incorporate components that are themselves bones of thcorctical contention.
'The model should be robust (i.c., compatible with a wide range of alternative assumptions about human information processing).
The spccifications wc arc about to present are simple and robust in this sense, and, indeed, summarizc thc core that is common to most current information processing theories of cognition.
Of course they are not entirely neutral, for they would be hard to rcconcile with an extreme form of behaviorism that denicd the relevance of central processes to the explanation of behavior.
But thcy arc not spccific to the view of any particular "sect" within the gencral information-processing tradition.
(For fuller discussion of the model, see Newell and Simon (1972, Chaptcr 14). and Simon (1979, Chapters 2, 3).

## General
Specification The most general and weakest hypothesis we rcquire is that human cognition is information processing: that a cognitive proccss can be scen as a sequence of internal states successively transformcd by a series of information processes.
An important, and morc spccific, assumption is that information is stored in several mcmorics having differcnt capacities and accessing charactcristics: sevcral scnsory stores of very short duration, a short-term memory (ST'M) with limitcd capacity and/or intermediate duration, and a long-term memory (l'TM) with very large capacity and rclatively pcrmancnt storage, but with slow fixation and access times compared with the other memorics.
Within the framcwork of this information proccssing model, it is assumed that information recently acquircd (attended to or heeded)\* by the ccntral processor is kept in STM, and is directly accessible for further processing (c.g., for producing verbal rcports), whcrcas information from LIM must first be retricved (transfered to SIM) before it can be reported.
'This general picture is compatible with all sorts of spccific hypotheses that have becn put forth with respect to thc dctails of the mechanisms.
For examplc, some thcorists proposc that what we call "short-term memory" is not a scparatc, specialized store but simply a portion of I'lM that is currently and temporarily activated (Anderson, 1976).
Some theorists bclieve that information in ST'M cxtinguishcs with passagc of time, unless rehcarscd; othcrs that it is lost only when replaced.
In general, these differenccs of detail do not affect the model at the level of spccificity required for our purposes.
'The important hypothcsis for us is that, due to the limited capacity of STM, only the most reccntly heeded information is accessible directly.
However, a portion of the contents of STM are fixatcd in LTM before being lost from STM, and this portion can, at later points in timc, somctimes bc retrieved from LTM.
Our specification of thc system is gencral, but it is not vague.
Specific information processing models that incorporate thesc features have been constructed in the form of computer programs, and these have been shown to produce a varicty of bchaviors previously obscrved in psychological laboratories.
Verbal predictions of how such a system behaves can, thereby, bc testcd by using a computer program as a simulator.
The principal modcl of this kind that guides our own thinking about these processes is the EPΛM program, duc to Feigenbaum (1963) and Simon, and discussed in some detail in Section 3 of Simon (1979).
We assume that any verbalization or verbal rcport of the cognitive processes would have to be based on a subsct of the information held in ST'M and I'T'M.

## Detailed
Specification We now specify more fully the componcnts of the information processing systcm that we have just skctchcd.
'The model draws upon a variety of sources that are summarized in Newell and Simon (1972, Ch.
14) and Simon (1979, Ch.
2.3).
Few of the model's specifications arc controversial.
It makes no rcal diffcrencc, for example, whcthcr we assumc a single homogeneous memory with different modes of activation (e.g.
Anderson, 1976; Shiffrin & Schncider, 1977) or several discrete memory stores (scnsory stores, STM, and l'IM).
The important matters, which can bc described in cither terms, relate to thc amounts and kinds of information that can be retaincd, and the conditions for accessing them and reporting them verbally.
We will usc thc conventional model of multiple memories in our description.
Recognition.
Information rcceived from the sensory organs resides for a short time in memories (iconic and echoic mcmories) associated with the different senses.
During this time, portions of the sensory information are directly recognized and encodcd with thc aid of information already stored in ITM.
Recognition associates the stimulus, or some part of it, with existing patterns in LTM, and stores in SI'M "pointers" to those familiar patterns.
(T’he EPΛM discrimination net is a model of this recognition mechanism.) Intermcdiatc stages of thc direct rccognition process (the successive steps of discrimination), which may take only 10 to 100 msec, do not use STM to store their products.
Long-Term Memory.
The I'l'M may be picturcd as an enormous collection of interrelated nodes.
Nodes can be accessed cither by recognition (through the discrimination nct), as just explained, or by way of links that associate these nodes to othcrs that have already becn accessed.
Information accessed in cither way is then represented by pointers in STM.
Thus, information can be brought into ST'M from sensory stimuli via the recognition process, or from L'TM via the association process.
Association processes arc much slower than direct recognition processes, rcquiring at lcast several hundred msec for each associative step.
Associative processes may use SIM to store intermediatc stcps.
So, for cxample, in recalling a namc that is not immediately accessiblc, a person may usc a sequence of cues to find an associative path, step by step, to the sought-for name.
Such processes may last tens of seconds, or even minutes, and may leave numerous intcrmediate symbols in SI'M, where they are temporarily available for verbal reports.
Short-term Memory.
Thc central processor (CP), which controls and rcgulates the non-automatic cognitive processes, dctermines what small part of the information in scnsory stimuli and lT'M finds its way into SIM.
This is the information that is heeded or allended to.
'The amount of information that can reside in SI'M at one time is limited to a small numbcr (four?) of familiar patterns (chunks).
Each chunk is represented by one symbol or pointer to information in l.TM (Simon 1979, Ch.
2.2).
As new information is hecded, information previously stored in STM may be lost.
When a cognitive task (c.g., mental addition of a column of figures) is being carried out, the typical chunks in SlM are pointers to the opcrands, operators, and outputs of the operations that are being performed.
'Thus, in adding 3 to 4, pointers corresponding to the symbols "3," "4," "Pl.US," and "7" might at somc time bc prescnt in Sl'M.
Since, in our culture, adding two digits involves a direct reference to lTM ("table lookup"), no further dctail of the process would be hecded in STM or available for verbal reports.
On the other hand, if the task were to multiply 17 by 45, S'I'M might hold, at various points in the process "45," "17," "7," "TIMES," "3" (the carry in multiplying 45 by 7), "315" (the first intermcdiatc product), "45," "1," "TIMES," "PLUS," "765." We hold no brief for the details of the above description, which is intended mcrely as an examplc of the kinds of information wc would expect to be hecded in STM, and to be available, potentially, for concurrent or retrospective reports.
The spccific details would depend on the particular strategies subjects uscd and the nature of the chunks they had stored in lTM (Simon, 1979, Ch.
2.4).
ST'M would symbolize the process only down to some modest level of detail (corresponding to clementary processes of a sccond or two in duration), and we would not expect to find information there about simple, automated processes (e.g. the processes of retrieval from LTM or recognition processes), much less about neuronal events.
Thus, the architccture of the control apparatus (CP) detcrmines the fineness of grain of the representation of processes in STM.
Control of Attention.
T'he flow of attention is diverted, from time to time, by interruptions through the higher control mcchanism.
Intermediate stages in these interruptions, not being symbolized in STM, are not reportable.
Sudden movements in pcripheral vision, loud noises, emotions operating through the reticular systcm are important causes of interruption and shift in attention (Simon, 1979, Ch.
1.3).
While information heeded immediately bcfore or after a shift in attention may sometimes allow subjects to give a relatively clear account of the interruption, we would expect such information to be less complete than reports of an orderly process that is induced by the successive content of SI'M itself (c.g., a thought scqucnce during which goals in S'l'M are guiding the thought processes).
Fixation.
New information is retained in S'T'M during the time the CP is attending to it.
In order to crcatc an IT'M representation of new information that can later be recalled, associations must be built up by coding and imaging, as well as new tests and branches in thc recognition network.
These learning processes, including the storage of new information in l'l'M and the addition of ncw pathways in thc discrimination nct for acccssing it, are modeled in some dctail by EPΛM (Simon, 1979, Scction 3).
Processing of the order of 8 to 10 scconds is required to asscmble each new chunk from its familiar componcnts in ST'M, and to store it in LTM as a new chunk (Simon, 1979, Chs.
2.2, 2.3).
Automation.
As particular proccsses bccome highly practiced, they become more and more fully automated.
(Shiffrin & Schneider, 1977).
Automation means that intermcdiate stcps arc carricd out without being interprctcd, and without thcir inputs and outputs using STM.
'The automation of performance is thcrefore quite analogous to executing a computer algorithm in compiled instead of interpretive mode.
Automation (and compiling) have two important consequcnces.
Thcy greatly spced up the process (typically, by an ordcr of magnitude) and they make thc intermcdiate products unavailable to STM, hence unavailable also for verbal reports.

## Concluding
Remarks Our examination of two of the most vigorous challenges to the uscfulness of verbal reporting leaves intact our bclief that such reports— cspecially concurrent reports, and retrospcctive reports of specific cognitive processes—provide powerful mcans for gaining information about such processes.
T’he concurrent report reveals the sequencc of information heeded by the subject without altering the cognitive process, while other kinds of verbal reports may change these processcs.
In retrospective reports of spccific processes, subjects gencrally will actually retricve the trace of the processes.
In other forms of retrospcctive reporting, subjects, instead of recalling this information, may report information that they have inferred or otherwise gencrated.
Hence, in the chapters that follow, we will pay particular attcntion to the two spccial forms of reporting—the one concurrent, the other retrospcctive—that are most likcly to yield direct evidence of cognitive processes.

## Watson's
Attack on Introspection Just at a time when the classical introspectionists were becoming increasingly sclf-conscious about mcthodological issues (Titchencr, 1912a, 1912b, 1913), Watson (1913), in thc influential papcr "Psychology as the Behaviorist Vicws it," launchcd a total attack on thc study of consciousncss.

## SUMMARY
AND PROSPECT In this introductory chaptcr, we have set forth the hypothesis that verbal behavior is to be accounted for in the same way as any other behavior, that is, by developing and testing an information-processing model of

Protocol Analysis how information is accessed and vcrbalized in response to stimuli.
We have surveyed a wide range of differcnt vcrbal reporting tasks to show how they can be accommodatcd within this framework, and to show how we can use our model to resolve some of the controversies that have arisen about the interpretation of verbally reported information.
In the remainder of thc book, wc will focus largcly upon a few kinds of verbal rcports, particularly thinking-aloud protocols and immediate retrospective reports, that reflect the cognitive processes in the most dircct way.
Wc will survcy, as comprehcnsivcly as wc can, the litcraturc on such reports in order to show how they can be uscd as valid data about cognitive processes and structures.
In principle, our analysis is not limited to reports of these particular kinds, but it will also serve as a foundation for thc understanding of other rcporting tasks and procedures.
Wc will excludc studies of very unconstraincd tasks (fantasizing, imaging, free association) and most clinical studies.
We do not consider oursclves sufficiently familiar with clinical theory to intcrpct it using information processing terms.
Furthcrmore, two recent books have done a good job of discussing this litcrature (Kendall & Hollon, 1981; Merluzzi, Glass & Genest, 1981).
Wc havc not made any other conscious exccptions or exclusions, and have tricd hard to capture all the relevant literature within the bounds of our enterprise.
The next chaptcr will discuss the effects of verbalization upon task performance, and will show that instructions to think aloud do not alter the sequence of cognitive processes significantly.

Chapter 4, which discusses the issucs of cpiphcnomcnality and idiosyncracy of verbal reports, will demonstrate that verbally reported information is as regular and valid as other types of data.
Chapter 5 prcscnts a detailed model of verbalization processes under think-aloud and talk-aloud instructions.
Chapter 6 uses the theorctical model of verbalization to examine and evaluate coding schemcs and procedurcs, and to describe methods of analysis that are reliable and valid.
Chapter 7, the final chapter, provides a number of dctailed examples of various ways in which protocol analysis can be carricd out within our infornationprocessing framework. # EFFECTS OF VERBALIZATION We must now consider verbalization in the context of our gencral model of memory.
Information may reach, and be stored in, memory in a varicty of cncodings—visual, auditory, tactile.
In first approximation, at lcast, the aural (afferent) encoding and the articulatory (cfferent) encoding of oral language can both bc represented as strings of phonemes.
Without trying to decide whether the cncodings are identical or simply ncarly isomorphic, let us designate both as the oral encoding.
Now our fundamental assumption is that, when thc CP attends to or activates a structure in mcmory that is orally cncoded, then this structure can at the same time be vocalized overtly without making additional demands on proccssing time or capacity.
At any time when the contents of STM are words (i.e., arc orally encoded), we can spcak those words without interference frorn or with the ongoing processes.

## VERBALIZATION
AND THINKING In a varicty of situations, adults have been obscrved to speak aloud spontancously without intent to communicate.
An interesting cxample of this is given by Sperling (1967), who found that his subjects vocalized during presentation of visual (verbal) stimuli and during a waiting pcriod until delayed recall, especially in the presence of external noisc.
He proposed that in response to the visual presentation a corresponding articulatory code was activated and cxccuted, leaving an internal auditory trace which was stored in the normal auditory sensory store.
When noise was present, the articulation was made overt, thus entering the auditory sensory store by thc external route as well.
In the noise condition of a similar study by Hintzman (1965), the subjects did not report awareness of their overt verbalizations, suggesting that little or no additional processing was required for them, and possibly that the suppression of vocalization is monitored by feedback.
Spontaneous vocalization or noticeable silent articulation have bcen observed in studies of rather different cognitive activities, for example, in routine work under exposure to noisc (Morgan, 1916), in reading difficult passages, espccially in foreign languages (Gibson & l.evin, 1975), and in memorizing (Bartlett, 1932).
Even whcn the verbalization is not audible or the articulation directly obscrvable, thcrc is evidence for oral encoding of the stored information.
Confusion errors in immediate recall of visually presented verbal stimuli are similar to thosc obtained from auditory prescntation of the same stimuli, which suggcsts that they are stored in a similar (i.e. oral) code (Conrad, 1967; Estcs, 1973; Hintzman, 1965).
Although spontaneous vocalization provides evidence for a close relation between internal activation of orally coded information and the corresponding vocalization, we are skeptical of Watson's proposition (Watson, 1920), that thought is internalized speech.
It is more likely that internal activation may occur without periphcral activation—which would mean that the overtly verbalized information is a subset of the internally activated oral information.
In thc discussion of central versus peripheral thought, evidence from a number of studies makes the notion of a peripheral locus highly implausible.
Thorson (1925) found no structural relation between tongue movemcnts during vocalization of a word and tongue movements observed in subjects instructed to think about the same word.
However, Max (1934) attributed 'Thorson's results to lack of sensitivity and resolution of his recording techniques.
More modern techniques for recording EMG activity of the speech-producing organs show a pattern of results consistent with measurements of covert speech processes (McGuigan, 1970; Sokolov, 1972).
By feeding EMG activity back, Hardyck and Pctrinovich (1970) showed that subjects could learn to read without EMG activity in the speech organs, at least with simpler texts.
(With more difficult texts comprehension was poorcr with suppression of EMG.) Cole and Young (1975) found with a similar training procedure that subjects can learn to suppress EMG activity during a memory task without change in the processes involved.
According to thc hypothesis of a peripheral locus for thought, it should be possible to eliminate task-relevant thought by occupying the vocal system with reciting irrclevant phonemic patterns, like "la-la-la ..." or "hiya-hiya ..." Indced, in an early rcview Pintner (1913) noted in many studies a marked decrement in performance caused by such concurrent verbalization.
However, Pintner (1913) showed in nis own experiments that, with practice, subjects could lcarn to count (i.c., recite 14, 15, 16, 17, 14, .….) while reading a passage without a dccrcment in recall for the content of the passage.
However, morc recent work by Levy (1975, 1977) clearly shows that concurrent counting markedly affccts mcmory for the text rcad, even after extensive practice.
In thcse studics the subjects were not only asked to recite digits ( in this case 1 through 10), but to do it as fast as they possibly could.
In our view, this does not demonstratc the peripherality of thought.
The processes required for the recitation occupy not only the vocal system but also the central systcm for activating oral information, and the time to activate internal information can plausibly be assumed to equal the time for overt production.
Thc dcmonstration (Smith, Brown, Toman, & Goodman, 1947) that curare, which inhibits all skeletal muscles (including those in the vocal system), has no effect on higherlevel thought processęs is further evidence against peripheral activation.
We will now examine our model more closely in terms of (1), the peripheral activity of the vocal systems and the receiving sensory systems and (2) the internal activation of orally coded information.

## Interference
From Auditory Stimulation First, since our model assumes that the activated oral code resides in a portion of the auditory memory system, we would expect, at least under some conditions, interference from simultaneous auditory stimulation while retrieving such information during rchcarsal.
Poulton (1977) suggested that effects of noise on performance in many studies may be due to a masking of inncr spccch.
Thc obscrvations prescntcd carlier, that many subjects tend to vocalize noticably in noise to improve the signalto-noise ratio, support Poulton's hypothesis.
In tasks involving only maintenance of items in STM, some studies have found no effects of white noise (Hintzman, 1965; Murray, 1965).
Poulton showed that such results are consistcnt with intensified rchcarsal as a response to noise, and noted that in a study by Hamilton, Hockcy and Rejman (1977) the noise condition was advantagcous only for the most recently presented digits and disadvantageous for earlier presented digits.
Colle and Welsh (1976) proposed that white noise doesn't have an effect because it is not phoncmically encoded, and demonstrated that short-term recall was impaired by having subjccts listen to phoncmically encodable noise (i.e., irrclevant German).
From studies of selective attcntion to diffcrcnt spcakers (c.g., the cocktail-party phcnomcnon), we know that a listener can scparate spcakers on the basis of location and pitch.
Introspcctive reports of subjects in a study by Webcr and Bach (1969) suggest that the internal rchcarsal is perccived to bc of high pitch and to be locatcd in the "middle of the head." Colle and Wclsh propose that discrimination for location and pitch could explain thc differences in interfercncc obtained by Crowder (1973) bctwecn consonants and vowels.
Furthermore, thcse cucs may be uscd by subjects to differentiate covert and ovcrt rchearsal, when they arc not maskcd by external noise.

## Irrelevant
Covert and Overt Articulations The second empirically testable implication of our information processing model has to do with interference between the covert and overt articulations.
If there is a unitary mcchanism for activating orally coded information, it should be possible to occupy this mechanism with accessory tasks.
A wide range of differcnt tasks requiring irrelevant concurrent verbalization have been used to study the effects on task-directed processes.
As a complete review of all these studies is impossible here, we will simply make three points.
First, most studies are not very explicit as to what type of information processing would actually be required to generate the prescribed concurrent verbalizations, and what role the internal activation of oral information has. ln some cases (e.g., Estes, 1973) the information to be vcrbalized concurrently is presented visually, and thus requires both attention and recoding in order to activate the oral code.
When, as is usually the case, the information to bc verbalized is available in LTM, it becomes important whether the information forms a single chunk, or is part of a familiar list (e.g., the alphabct or the natural numbcrs), or a list of so many items that it constitutes scvcral chunks requiring successive retricval.
'The observed decrease with practice in interference from concurrcnt verbalizing might result from the sequence to be verbalized having been chunked.
The rate of verbalization is also a crucial variable.
Maximum interference would be expected when the rate of overt verbalization parallels thc rate of internal activation.
Another important condition is a requircment to verbalize items at a regular pace, which would eliminate the possibility of internal activation of larger speech units and most likely require additional processing.
Second, some important processes involving internal activation of oral codes are reduced or totally inhibited by certain concurrent verbalization tasks.
Levy (1975) showcd that rapid concurrent recital of numbers decreased recoding of visually presented verbal information.
Her data showed clear differences in memory for text betwcen groups of concurrently verbalizing subjccts given auditory and visual prescntations, respectively.
Recoding of visually prcscnted digits into oral code was climinated when subjccts pronounced visually displayed numbers (Estes, 1973) and when they recited nonscnse words (I evy, 1971).
Rehcarsal of orally coded information disappcared (Baddeley, 'Thomson, & Buchanan, 1975) when subjects concurrently counted from 1 to 8 at a regular rate of three digits per second.
'Third, overt verbalizatioı: of non-oral information is impeded by tasks rcquiring extensive rehearsal of orally codcd information.
In a series of experiments Brooks (1968) dcmonstrated that when subjccts had to make word category judgments (e.g., "noun" or "article") for each word in a scntence, they took longer to make verbal responses (i.e.
"yes" or "no") than to point to visually available response words.
The fact that the subjects had to maintain the surface form of the relatively long (tenword) sentences in memory was crucial, for the effects disappeared when the sentcnces remained visually available during the ouput of the word category decisions.
The verbal labels associated with the word category judgments had to use the same limited-capacity ST'M system as the rehcarsal of the words of the scntence and the information for keeping track of the next word to be categorized.

## Time
Requirements for Vocalization A third implication of our model is that, in activating the oral code, articulation and vocalization follow without requiring additional time.
If the code is oral, there is thus not any difference in time taken for overt and silent rehearsal or activation.
'There are some suggestions (Gibson & Levin.
1975) that, due to the redundancy of languagc and verbal structures, inncr spcech may not rcquirc complete articulation.
In most available relevant studies, complete internal activation in the silent case is assurcd by using non-redundant oral code or by instructing the subject. ln a frequently citcd study, I.andaucr (1962) found that implicit recitation spced for well-lcarncd lists likc the alphabet, the sequence of natural numbers, and the pledgc of allegiancc was no different from overt recitation spced, espccially after practicc in overt vcrbalizing.
Weber and Bach (1969) found no difference in spccd bctwcen rccitation of thc alphabct silently and aloud, and thcir study showcd no practice effects ovcr a scquencc of tcn trials.
Chase (1977) found that overt rchearsal of letter combinations was about 15 percent slower than covert rchcarsal, rcquiring an additional 30 msec per lettcr, but suggested that further practice might climinate that differcnce.
In a study of metered memory scarch, Webcr and Blagowsky (1970) found that instructing one group of subjects to verbalizc the intermcdiate stcps (i.c., the list items betwecn the stimulus item and the response) produccd no differences in performance and latencies, as compared with silent control subjects and subjects instructed to say the steps silently to themselves.

## EXPERIMENTAL
STUDIES OF VERBALIZING WITHOUT RECODING The model we have described implics that verbalization will not interfere with ongoing processes if the information stored in STM is encoded orally, so that an articulatory code can readily be activated.
The implications of the model can be tested in a wide variety of situations where the subject is explicitly called upon to verbalize.
We will begin by examining studies where the tasks are fairly simple in structure and whcre evidence is available to suggest strongly a spontaneous oral encoding of the information.
Such cvidcnce includes data on confusion errors in rctention and indications of spontaneous vcrbalization, as well as information about how the task was originally lcarned.
For example, in the carly learning of many skills—like reading and arithmctic—performance of the task is accompanied by overt verbalization.
After a discussion of these studies, wc will turn to thinkingaloud studies of more complcx tasks, where we have less knowledge about how the task information in S'I'M is cncoded.

## Simple
Tasks With Oral Codes In the tasks considered in this section, the subject is instructed to retain information presented to him.
Since the information is presented by the experimenter, we know that it can be heedcd, and we can make reasonable assumptions as to how it is encoded internally.
Typically, the subject is presented with letters, digits, or words, which wc have assumed will be hcld in S'T'M in an oral encoding.
Under these conditions, verbalization should be cffortless, and should not interferc with task performance.
However, in most studies, thc instruction is not just to verbalize the stimulus information, but to produce specified verbalizations based on it (e.g., to read the stimuli aloud one by onc, to rchcarse the stimuli aloud when they arc presented, ctc.) Λs any changc in the sequence and frequency with which information is heedcd by thc subject will change the cognitive process, we must scrutinize the verbalization instructions as to their effects on attention.
The requested verbalizations may be selective and result in selective attention to thc stimulus displays, especially when there are multiple stimuli.
Instructions to verbalize sometimes spccify the units of information to be verbalized, thus biasing attention towards those units.
For example, subjects instructed to verbalize individual digits in a stimulus sequence may pay less attention to patterns of digits than uninstructed subjects.
Instructions sometimes prescribe a short time interval for producing the verbalization, which may not correspond to the time during which this information would otherwisc be heeded.
The instructions sometimes prescribe the pace of verbalization, and thereby influence the duration of attention to each piece of information; this, in turn, may affect processes associated with fixating information in LTM.
Furthermore, an instruction to kecp a fast pace may bias the subject to retricve information from STM as opposed to LTM because of the differcntial retrieval times for the two stores.
In the following studies, unless the contrary is explicitly mentioned, the inter-stimulus intervals are identical between the verbalizing and the silent group.
This means that the time available for subjects in the two groups is identical, so that pcrformance can be compared directly in terms of amount of information retained, and so forth.

## Vocalization
at Presentation In the present section, we study memory-span tasks where stimuli are presented rapidly and recalled almost immediately.
There is strong evidence that, in response to a visual prescntation of a verbal stimulus, an oral encoding is normally activatcd (c.g., Conrad, 1967; Estcs, 1973; Hintzman, 1965) and thus could be vocalized.
When subjects vocalize visual stimuli, immediate rccall for the lastpresented items is improved over the silent condition (Conrad & Hull, 1968; Crowdcr, 1970; Murray, 1965; Routh, 1970).
'Thc samc cffect is found if the experimcnter, instcad of thc subject, verbalizes the stimulus, as well as under the condition of auditory presentation (Crowder, 1970; Penney, 1975).
Since visual stimuli arc, by the assumptions of our model, also orally encodcd, this "modality effect" suggests that it is not the encoding of the stimulus, but hearing and storing an articulation of it, that enhances recall of the reccnt items.
'This interpretation is supported by studics by Murray (1965) and Tell (1971), which show that the magnitude of the effect depends on the degree of articulation (e.g., whispering versus pronunciation aloud).
Murray did not find any difference between silent articulation (i.e., mouthing) and the non-articulating control group.
Furthermore, Levy (1971) showed that mouthing did not produce as large an effect as auditory presentation.
'T’hus, the effect of vocalizing visual stimuli appears to be due primarily to the auditory feedback from vocalizing.
Let us now look at this effect in more detail.
The effect on immediate recall of vocalizing with visual presentation is largest with fast prescntation rates (Murray, 1965) and decreases when there is irrelevant interpolated verbal activity (Crowder, 1970; Tell, 197l).
For normal presentation rates and vocalization of cach stimulus, the effect is limited to the last couple of stimulus items (Conrad & Hull, 1968; Crowder, 1970).
A somewhat longer effective range has been observed for recognition tasks (McNabb & Massaro in Massaro, 1975).
A more complete discussion of the range and character of the modality effect is presented in Penney (1975).
Vocalizing stimuli at presentation can have at least two other effects.
First, sometimes vocalizing produces worse performance than silence.
When the visual stimuli are not presented individually, but simultaneously in groups, subjects in the silent condition perform better (Penney, 1975; Slak, 1969).
In these expcrimcnts, the vocalizing subjects are instructed to pronounce the stimuli one by one (i.e., digit by digit), while the silent subjects can group the stimuli for their covert rehearsal.
Thus the instruction forces the verbalizing subjects to use an inferior coding format.
Second, some studies show a decrement in performance when subjects are instructed to vocalize auditory stimuli (Mackworth, 1964), and in particular, a decrement in retention of carly items (Crowder, 1970; Ellis, 1969).
In the case where the stimuli are prescnted orally, immediately reactivating the just-presented item to generate the required vocalization does not scem efficicnt, and probably occurs at the expense of other processing, like rehcarsal of carlier items.

## Verbalizing
Rehearsal Processes We turn now to experiments wherc the subject is instructed to rehearse aloud information held in memory.
Such rchcarsal may take place under two quite different circumstances: when the information rehearsed is being held in STM, and when the information is rchcarsed as an aid to fixating it in LTM.
The effects of these two kinds of rchearsal upon task performance may not be at all the same.
We must also consider the possibility that the subject may change his strategy to take advantage of the improvement in short-term retention produced by vocalization, and may by that change affect his performance of thc task.
'This is especially likely to happen when the instructions emphasize the requirement of vocalization rather than retention of the stimulus material.
In confronting our model with studies of the effects of verbalization, then, we must take careful account of the verbalization instructions given to the subject.
Three dimensions of variation in the instructions may be noted: (1) In some studies the subject is asked to rchearse or pronounce words at a specified pace, while in other studies, he is instructed simply to vocalize covert rehearsal (i.e., "to say out loud any word on the list he was thinking about while hc was thinking about it") (Geisclman & Bellezza, 1977).
(2) In several studies the subject is constraincd to rehearse only the items presented, or some subset of them.
A more subtle and common restriction is to constrain the subject to vcrbalize individual stimulus items, instead of recoding them as higher-level chunks.
Although in a few studies subjects were explicitly told that therc were no restrictions on their encodings of list items (Brodie, 1975; Brodie & Murdock, 1977), recoding would still imply a discrepancy between the verbalized information and the internal encoding.
(3) Last, but not least important, subjects are generally required to rehearse or verbalize frequently (Horton, 1976), or instructcd to fill the presentation interval with thcir rehcarsals (Einstcin, Pellcgrino, Mondani, & Battig, 1974; Kellas, McCaulcy & McFarland, 1975; Rundus, 1971; Rundus & Atkinson, 1970).
Even without such instructions, the observed rate of rchcarsal is rather high, around 1 rchcarscd item per second (Brodie & Murdock, 1977; Geiselman & Bellezza, 1977).
Since retricval from long-tcrm memory is known to take considcrable time—of the order of scconds (Simon, 1974) —one might anticipate that a requirement of frequent rchcarsing would bias the subjcct toward retrieving items from SI'M.
Wc might also anticipatc a bias toward maintaining information in STM, which is achicvablc by rchcarsing items serially.
This would likely improve performance on short lists, but degrade performance on longer lists.
Analyzing the results of Brodie and Murdock (1977), Kintsch and Polson (1979) noticed that subjccts sclccted items for continued rehearsal inefficiently and rehearsed some items much longer than would be necessary for the memory performance.
It would be informative if studies recording rehearsals would analyze the temporal structure and selection of items, but such information is seldom reported.
Other indices of the rchearsal process, like eye fixations, have been found to vary with instructions for overt rehearsal (Geiselman & Bcllezza, 1977).
It has been suggested that, under additional instructions regulating their verbalizations, subjects will rchearse list items scrially more often than will control subjccts (Kellas et al., 1975).
In support of this hypothesis, Kellas et al. found that differcnces in study time between verbalizing subjects and controls decrcascd substantially when recall conditions were changed from free to serial recall.
They also found that, in free recall, verbalizing subjects followed the serial order of the stimuli more closely than controls did.
Murray (1967) found that differences in performance were much smaller with forced serial recall than with semifree recall.
Geiselman and Bellezza (1977), using simultaneously presented items, found their verbalizing subjects were better than controls at recalling the two leftmost items, a rcsult which they interpreted as evidence for more serial processing among the formcr.
In an interesting developmental study, Kellas et al.
(1975) found no differcnce between verbalizing and control subjccts for students bclow the 7th grade.
They interpreted this finding as marking thc age at which childrcn first acquire the more sophisticated encoding strategies, which would give an advantage to the control subjects.
The hypothesis, that the verbalizing subjects with a bias toward serial rehearsal would have an advantage in recall of short lists and a disadvantage in recall of longer lists, gets some support from the fact that Geiselman and Bellezza (1977) found superior recall with verbalization for a list of 8 simultaneously presented items; Horton (1976) and Roenker (1974) found no difference in immediate rccall for lists of 12 and 15 items; while Fischlcr, Rundus & Atkinson (1970) and Finstein et al.
(1974) found a significant dccremcnt with verbalization in recall of lists of 20 and 24 items.
It should bc notcd that in Roenkcr's study the words were prescnted auditorily, which might reduce the diffcrence in proccssing between vocalization and control conditions; in all the other studies, the words wcre presented visually.
'There is some evidence that how much information will be stored in L'TM, and how much will be retained in S'I'M, dcpcnds on the modality (visual or auditory) in which the stimuli are presented (Penney, 1975).
Geiselman and Bellezza (1977) found that when subjects were informed that they would be asked to remcmber the stimulus items for delayed recall, their rates of verbalizing droppcd by 30 percent.
This suggests that an intention to fixate information in lTM leads to slower rehearsal, and furthermore, that regulating the rate of verbalizing and rehearsing by instruction may produce significant processing differences.
In a study comparing covert and overt rehearsal (Brclsford & Atkinson, 1968), recall of paired associates was invcstigated with a continuous presentation technique.
Verbalizing subjects showed a clear advantage over controls for lags betwecn prescntation and recall of paired-associate items up to five or six items, that is, about up to the span of ST'M.
This result is consistent with a strategy, among the verbalizers, of maintaining information primarily in STM to allow easier updating.
There are several experiments where the instruction to verbalize was used to control rather than simply monitor rehcarsal processes.
In a study on incidcntal learning, Mechanic (1964) showed that instructions to repeat the pronunciation of the stimuli aloud increased retention.
Even more interesting, he showed that, using the same pronouncing procedure, instructions to memorize the words did not improve retention.
Howcver, subjects not requircd to use thc pronunciation procedure retained the material better with an instruction to memorize than without it.
In several studies (Einstcin et al., 1974; Fischler ct al., 1970; Glanzer & Meinzer, 1967), where subjects were instructed to vocalize frequently or to rehearse the just-presented item, their recall was always much poorer than that of controls.
In two of these studies, the more intriguing comparison can be made betwcen overt rehearsal of any item and restricted overt rehearsal.
In Fischler et al., the overall performance is about the same in both conditions.
In Einstein et al., using a somewhat longer list, the recall is somewhat better under conditions of restricted verbalization.
These results would again be expccted because of the difference between processing that is dirccted toward fixating information in LTM and processing that maintains information in ST'M.
Undcr the restricted rehcarsal condition, we would cxpcct subjects to encodc in I TM the item being rchcarscd rcpcatedly, while with unrestrictcd rchcarsal, they would tend to maintain the items in STM.
Such a difference in strategy would produce the observed relative advantage of the LT'M encoding strategy with longer lists of items.

## Verbalizing
With Multiple Stimulus Displays Not all the studies discussed below usc verbalizations directly to monitor the cognitive activity.
But since they specify rather clearly the verbalizations required of the subject, they will serve to illustrate some of the effects of such procedures.
With one exccption (Geisclman & Bellezza, 1977), the studies discussed carlier have prescntcd one stimulus at a time, so that problems of competition of attention among different stimuli can be disrcgarded.
The most direct example of multiple stimuli is discrimination learning with two stimuli. ln a study on discrimination learning with words, Wilder (1971) found that rcquiring subjects to utter the correct choice aloud led to faster learning of the list of discriminations.
From our carlier discussion it would be reasonable to assume that hearing one's own voice and clicitcd associations may be a uscful mcmory cuc for recognizing thc correct response on subsequent trials.
This was possible with a relatively small number of responses per list (l6) and a rclatively short interval between recurring discrimination items, for the prescntation of the list took about a minute.
Ghatala, Lcvin and Subkoviak (1975) showed that the same increase in performance as found for subjects verbalizing the correct items could be obtained by instructing subjects to use imagery.
A similar study was conducted by Carmcan and Weir (1967) with visually presented drawings as stimuli.
An instruction to describe or name the visually portrayed objcct should require a verbally coded name to be generated for the object.
One might arguc that stimuli like those used in this experiment automatically elicit a verbally coded name, but this cannot be taken for granted in the gencral casc.
In this study subjects were instructed to vocalize the name of the visual stimulus according to five different instructions.
'l’he degree of correlation (either positive or ncgative) betwcen the correct response and the overtly named stimulus, which was regulated by the different instructions, was strongly related to the spced of learning in the discrimination task.
In the immediate recall, a clear rclation was found bctwcen the stimuli vcrbalized and stimuli recalled, and an overall better rccall was found for thc verbalizing conditions as compared to the control condition.
'T’hese general results have been replicated by Weir and Hclgoe (1968).
T'he rclation between verbalizing names of visually displaycd objects and long term retention (onc wcck) was investigatcd in a now classic study by Kurtz and Hovland (1953).
'The subjects were prescnted with a four-by-four matrix of objects, which were sclected so that subjects could label them without ambiguity.
In the control condition the experimenter would point to one of the objccts and ask the subject to make a circle around that object on a photo of thc stimulus.
Whcn the cxperimenter pointed to an object in the experimental condition, the subjccts were to find the name of the object in a four-by-four matrix of namcs arranged exactly like the matrix of objccts, encircle thc word and pronounce it overtly.
When the subjects werc, a weck later, given a recognition test or a written test of recall, the experimental group showed superior retention on both tests.
In evaluating the effective clemcnt in the above procedure, a study by Rosenbaum (1962) is heipful.
It differed from the others mainly in that the control group cncirclcd words in the matrix and thus behaved just as the experimental group did, apart from the pronounciation of the word.
Rosenbaum found subjects pronouncing the word to have superior retention on tests of recognition and recall, and furthcrmore, silent subjects exposed to somebody else's pronounciation to show a similar increase in retention.
Even though it can be argued that thc structural isomorphism of objects and words could have made it possible to do the task without cognizing the word, the primary cause of thesc changes in retention is not likely to be the clicitation of a verbal intcrnal code, especially not with carcfully sclcctcd objects.
From thcsc results, we infer that the causal agent in thcse studies is not the production or generation of the overt verbalization but rather the internal processes elicited in response to the instructions to verbalize.

## Verbalizing
Associated With Mental Arithmetic In mental addition and multiplication, the subjects are presented either visually or orally with numbcrs and the mathematical operators and must generate the answer without recourse to external memory.
There is convincing evidence from the way these skills are learned that the internal code of the numbers, operations and internally gencrated products is cither uscd or readily elicited.
Our modcl predicts that it should be possible for the subiccts to verbalize the heeded information, especially as all new mental content is generated scqucntially.
'T’hc available studies on the effects of the instruction to verbalizc are sparse and will be dealt with individually.
A study on mental arithmctic by Wegner (Merz, 1969) investigated the existence and possible nature of the effect of verbalizing.
To separate the effects due to producing the vocalization from the effects due to hearing it, the subjects wore ear phoncs with a noise level that prevented them from hearing their own voices.
In one of the verbalization groups their amplified voices were superimposed on the noise, in the other they were not, thus eliminating the feedback of the voice.
It was found to be more difficult to instruct the subjects in the non-fecdback condition to refrain from verbalizing, which suggcsts that verbalizing is a normal behavior in such a noisy environment (Hintzman, 1965).
Feedback of the voice was found to be the crucial factor, as thcre was no improvement without it.
In the arithmetic task, three digits, which were available to the subject only one at time on a kind of memory drum, had to be subtracted from or added to each other.
Temporary storage of the intermediate results appeared to be the major difficulty, with feedback of the voice proving to be exceptionally helpful in at least two respects.
First, the subjects without feedback and the control subjects wcnt back more often to look at the digits presented earlier in the triple, which took additional time and led to completion of fewer problems.
Second, the subjects without fecdback obtained more incorrect subtotals than thc subjects with feedback.
In accord with the results presented earlier, hearing the overt verbalization seemed to be the important factor in improving short-term retention and performance.
Fryer (1941) was primarily interested in the role of articulation in automatic mental work.
In a number of experiments with a test involving writing down totals of very simple additions (the sums never exceeded nine), he found that instructing the subjects to refrain from articulation impeded performance markedly.
Retrospectively, subjccts judged it to be almost impossible to avoid articulation. lnstructing subjects to vocalize the answers before writing them down, or to whisper them silently led to a consistent and reliablc decrement in speed of performance.
However, since the average decrement was no more than about one percent, Fryer suggests that it may be attributed to the extra monitoring required to assure the articulation for each answer.
In a study of mental multiplication, Danscreau and Grcgg (1966) asked a subject to verbalize each step during the solution process.
Whenever the subject remained silent too long, the experimcnter would urge him to talk.
On a wide range of problems varying in difficulty, no reliable differences in spced of performance were found between a silent control condition and the verbalizing condition.
In spite of this finding, the subjects judged introspectively that verbalizing slowed down thc process but facilitated the necessary fixation and storage of intermediate results in memory.
In a subsequent study, Dansereau (1969) reports that, with in creased practice, two of his bctter subjects gave overt verbalizations only of intermediate results and the initial problem, and they reported introspectively that complete verbalization interfered with retrieving information.
Dansereau suggests that thesc subjects used overt verbalization as a retrieval cue for accessing important information.
'To what extent the subjects felt that verbalizing slowed thcm down is not reported, nor is a comparison provided with performance under a silent control condition.

## Some
Conclusions In nearly all the studies reviewed in this section, performance time was the same in verbalization and control conditions, both when trials were paced by the experimenter and when the subject determined the pace.
Our modcl, agrecing with thesc findings, prcdicts that overt verbalization under thinking-aloud instructions will not affect the speed of performance unless the verbalizations have to be qucued.
With a few possible exceptions, the empirical studies do not provide any evidence that queuing occurs.
We have identified few studies where subjects are simply instructed to verbalize the heeded information; in most studies, specific requirements are imposed on them with respect to the timing, frequency, and content of their verbalizations.
There is evidence that when subjects try to comply with such requirements, the normal course of their internal processes is altered (e.g., rote serial rehearsal may incrcase and attention may be shifted).
Apart from the effects of imposing specific rcquirements for verbalization, hcaring overt vcrbalizations generally facilitates memory retrieval and storage.
'I’he first componcnt of this effect is most likely the grcater durability of thc accoustical sensory storc, which only spans a couple of seconds and is furthermore subject to masking by subscquent verbalizations.
'The sccond, longer-term, componcnt is a facilitation in retrieval, due to the specific cucs supplicd accoustically by the overt verbalization.
'The strength of the sccond effect would depend on how selectivc the overt verbalizations wcre with respect to the retrieval task.
Increascs in the verbalization of matcrial other than that which was to be remembered should decrease this effect.

## THINKING-ALOUD
PROCESSES In the previous section we reviewcd experiments in which the subject was instructed to verbalizc or rchearse the actual stimuli.
Only in the arithmetic tasks was the subject required to verbalize thoughts that he himself generated in the course of performing a task.
We turn now to our main concern, thinking-aloud (TΛ) instructions, where the subject is specifically ask to vocalize those self-gencrated symbols while he performs his task.
Again, we will be seeking evidence on the extent to which the 'l'A activity affccts the performance of the main task.
Thinking-aloud activity is not entirely alien to evcryday life, and almost all subjects have probably had some experience of it before they come to the laboratory.
Students at school occasionally have to explain their solutions of problems aloud to their fellow studcnts in order to show how the solutions were generated.
In othcr situations, people explain or describe their solution attempts to others, so that the listener can tell them wherc their thinking is in error.
Even more frequently, people just communicate their thinking to others.
In many cases, at least, such verbalization requires considerable intermediatc processing prior to articulation, and is distinctly different from the verbalization of ongoing cognitive processes.
In order to characterize the differences, we will dcscribe three differcnt levels at which a subject can verbalize his thought processes and their content.

## Levels
of Verbalization 1.
A first level of verbalization is simply the vocalization of covert articulatory or oral encodings, as required in the tasks we have presented in the previous sections.
At this level, there are no intermcdiate processes, and the subject needs expend no special effort to communicate his thoughts.
A distinction must still be made, howcver, between cases where the subject is directing his communications to himself, and those wherc he wishes to communicate with othcr people.
'T'hc self-dirccted verbalizations have been found to be more idiomatic and to use more idiosyncratic referents than communications dirccted to others (Werner & Kaplan, 1963).
In which catcgory a particular example of vcrbalization falls may depend on the subject's intcrpretation of the instructions, as well as upon their actual content.
2.
A second level of verbalization involves description, or rather explication of the thought content.
We assign to this level verbalizations that do not bring new information into the focus of the subject's attention, but only explicate or label information that is held in a compressed internal format or in an encoding that is not isomorphic with language (e.g., information about odors).
We will have to add to our model the requisite recoding processes.
We will refer to verbalization requiring such recoding as Level 2 verbalization.
Since explication or recoding requires processing time for the subject but does not replace other processing involved in the task performance, a subject who is verbalizing at this second level can be expected to take more time for the task than one who is not verbalizing.
However, we would hypothesize that such recoding does not change the structure of the process for performing the main task.
3.
A third level of verbalization rcquires the subject to explain his thought processes or thoughts.
An explanation of thoughts, ideas, or hypotheses or their motives is not simply a rccoding of information already prescnt in STM, but requires linking this information to earlier thoughts and information attcnded to previously.
Level 2 verbalization does not encompass such additional interprctative processes.
If, in the normal course of task performance, a subject pays attention to the relational or gencrating processes that are bringing new information into his STM (and insofar as he can pay attention to them), the verbalization would fall within the compass of Level 2 verbalization.
But if the subject does not attend to these processes, then he will have to make intermediate inferences, which may or may not represent correctly his actual motives or the actual causes linking his thoughts.
Moreover, an instruction requiring a subject to explain his thoughts may direct his attention to his procedures, thus changing the structure of the thought process.

## Alternative
Thinking-Aloud Instructions The subject's TA protocol and (specifically whether it will correspond mainly to Ievels 1, 2, or 3) may well be influenccd by the exact wording of the TA instructions.
We will begin by examining the instructions given by the two psychologists, Duncker and Claparède, who are usually credited with introducing the method of thinking aloud.
In describing their instructions, we will distinguish a main part from some complementary parts.
The main part of the instruction to think aloud is usually very short, making reference to a procedure that is presumed to be already familiar to the subjects.
"Try to think aloud.
I guess you often do so when you are alonc and working on a problem." (Duncker, 1926; italics in original) "Think, reason in a loud voice, tell me everything that passes through your head during your work scarching for the solution to the problem." (Claparède, 1934.) Thus the subjects are asked just to vocalize their thoughts, which are apparently presumed to have the form of inner specch.
If the presumption is correct, it is not surprising that such short instructions could elicit the desired behavior.
Verbalizing, under this assumption, would be quite simple (Level 1), because of the oral code and sequential structure of the internal speech.
In Claperède's instructions, however, the subject is asked to verbalize "everything that passes through [his] head," whether encoded orally or not.
In order to comply with such an instruction, the subject would in many cases have to label and encode the content of STM, thus requiring the kinds of recoding processes that are postulated in Level 2 verbalization.
TA instructions frequently contain other information or requirements, which we have already refered to as "complementary." One complementary instruction that is often included is a request for completeness.
Here are two examples: "The chief thing is to talk aloud constantly from the minute I present the picturc, for I want to get everything you happen to think of, no matter how irrelevant it may seem.' (Patrick, 1935) "I am not primarily interested in your final solution, still less in your reaction timc, but in your thinking behavior, in all your attempts, in whatcver comes to your mind, no matter whether it is a good or a less good idca or a question.
Be bold!
I do not count your wrong attempts, therefore speak them all out." (Duncker, 1926; italics in original) 'l'here appear to be at least two ways in which this instruction could be implemented by a verbalization procedure: (a) A superordinate monitoring process could be incorporated in the proccdure to guarantee that every item would bc verbalized; (b) In quite an opposite direction, the effect of the instruction could be to eliminatc any censorship process intervening between awareness of S'l'M contents and thcir vocalization.
Some 'TA instructions imply the presence of, and require the climination of, such censorship: "Don't plan what to say or speak after the thought, but rather let your thoughts speak, as though you were really thinking out loud." (Silveira, 1972) Another kind of complementary instruction is a request for explanation.
In order to gct as full an understanding as possible of the subjects' processes, they are askcd to explain their thinking: "In order to follow your thoughts we ask you to think aloud, explaining each stcp as thoroughly as you can." (Smith, 1971) As follows from our earlier discussion, inducing the subject to explain his solution very likely changes the structure of his thought processes.
In a school situation with mathematics tasks, where thc students were accustomcd to cxplaining their solutions aloud, Krutetskii (1976) took special pains to warn his subjects against confusing the instruction to think aloud with that of explaining the solution: "Do not try to explain anything to anyone else.
Pretend there is no one here but yoursclf.
Do not tell about the solution but solve it." (Krutetskii, 1976) Relatively frequently, complemcntary instructions are included to influence the content of the verbalizations.
Investigators are sometimes specifically interested in certain types of mental content or mental processes, and ask their subjects to take spccial care to report instances of such content or processes (Johnson, 1964; Schecrer & Huling, 1960; Webb, 1975).
Othcr investigators have askcd subjccts to verbalize what they are doing physically as well as what they arc thinking (Hafner, 1957; Mayzner, Tressclt, & Hclbock, 1964).
Still other investigators have asked subjects to verbalizc what they arc pcrcciving visually (Farley, 1974; Hucsmann & Cheng, 1973).
In many of thcsc studics, the cxact wording of the instructions is not reported, which makcs it difficult to discuss what verbalization proccdurcs are necessary to comply with them.
In most cases, howcver, it would be nccessary to scan for spccific content and to cncodc it for vocalization whcn found.
Such monitoring would be, in fact, self-observation at the third level we described earlier.
One can only conjecture to what extent subjccts pay attention to, undcrstand, and comply with 'T'A instructions, espccially their complementary portions, and especially when thc instructions are only presented at the beginning of sessions that may bc an hour or more in length.
'There are many other conditions in a T∧ expcriment that may affect the verbalization procedures of subjects as much as or more than instructions do.
We turn next to these additional factors.

## Effects
of Training and Reminders In many TA cxperiments, the subject is given initial warm-up problems to acquaint him with the expcrimcntal situation and accustom him to the microphones and tape recorders.
In some studies, more extensive warmup procedures are uscd cxplicitly to train the subjects to conform to the TA instructions.
