The source cited most widely in support of the importance of unconscious processes is Poincarć (Ghisclin, 1952). Λ critical reading of Poincaré does not provide any evidence for unconscious processing, nor for the belief that Poincaré himself favored such an interpretation.
Poincarć, discussing mathematical crcation from the vicwpoint of a completely "logical" mind, makes some observations, strikingly similar to those currently emphasized by information processing psychology, about the limitations of humans.
He points to the limits of short-term memory as an explanation of occasional errors in generating proofs, and observes that the primary component of mathematical skill is a finer representation of mathemnatical knowledge that yields better effective memory, yet is restricted entirely to the mathematical domain.
Mathematical creation, according to Poincarć, is "making new combinations with mathcmatical cntitics alrcady known." Hc concludes that a mcchanical combination of all possible alternatives is practically impossible, because of the large number of alternatives and he asserts that mathematicians only consider combinations that have a potential for yiclding intercsting results: Never in the field of his consciousness do combinations appcar that are not really useful, cxcept some that he rejccts but which have to somne cxtent the characteristics of useful combinations.
(Poincaré, 1952, p.
25) Consistent with both of these observations is the view that the objects of mathematical thought arc abstract entitics and patterns rather than detailed realizations of strings of symbols and the like.
Poincaré (1952) describes some circumstances in which he had sudden insights into mathematical relations.
We note with interest that in the cases he cites, the insight involves seeing a correspondence between his current problem and some other devcloped domain of mathematics that was stored in, and accessible froin, his L'I'M.

He only mentions his memory of the general social situation in which the sudden insight occurred.
He makes the important observation that: These sudden inspirations ... never happen except after some days of voluntary effort which has appcared absolutely fruitless and where nothing good scems to have come, where the way takcn secms totally astray.
(Poincaré, 1952, p.
27) Further, the subjcctive fecling of certainty of the correctness of the solution is occasionally mistaken: We almost always notice that this falsc idca, had it been true, would have gratified our natural fecling for mathematical clegancc.
(Poincarć, 1952, p.
29) Although Poincaré considers the possibility that unconscious processing continues after the conscious work and delivers the resulting solution, he rejccts this proposal as unreasonable.
He points out that in no case do the "unconscious processes make any calculations." In his experience they simply point out the similarity of two existing structures in LTM.

30).
This model of the process is quite consonant with our model of problem solution by rccognition.
Poincaré's cxplanation requires no more unconscious processing than the unconscious steps in the recoguition proccss that we have discussed beforc.

## Regeneration—Hypotheses
Wc will argue that for the most part our bchavior is mediatcd by cognitive proceses that generate actively the responses that are sought.
'This is true cven when thc same task is presented repcatedly.
In many cases where the same behavior is required again and again, the conscious level of control is changed to a monitoring rolc, and the corresponding memory tracc may becomne weak or disappear.
In thc common case where one is wondering, for cxample, whcther one turned off the stove or locked the door to one's house, unless some cxplicit attempt was made to memorize this event or some deviation occurred from the normal course of events, one is generally unable to retrieve any episodic mnemory even a few scconds later.
Most people have returned to the door to check whethcr it was lockcd, and found it to bc so, which shows that the process was actually exccuted.
Even in situations with rather full retrospective reports, subjects often have difficulty in retricving the corresponding cpisodic memory.
However, this doesn't imply that they cannot give valid reports on "what thcy must have donc." When repcating thc samc task, like multiplying two 2-digit numbers in one's head, a subject is highly likely to encounter the same information cach time.
We might call memory of this information "regeneration memory" to distinguish it from memory of the individual episodes.
Regeneration memory, of course, is simply contained in LTM, and does not constitute a separate specialized memory.
For the most part, regencration memory provides a good source for determining how we did behave when the behavior concerns responses to invariant knowledge structures or stable aspects of the environment.
'T'he answers that subjects give to questions likc, "Name the current President of the United States," or "Give a word starting with 'A’," can be retricved from regeneration memory as well.
Regeneration memory would provide invalid reports if thc identity of the President had meanwhile been changed, or if some other word starting with "A" had occurred immediately bcfore.
'The possibility that subjects may be relying on regencration memory rather than cpisodic memory should be ascertainable through retrospcctive reports.
Wc believe that subjects are able to discriminate between the two types of memory.
However, there also are paradigms that will diffcrentiate the two.
It is possible to prcscnt the subject with incomplete information so as to climinate reprocessing, yet to present sufficicnt information to serve as a retrieval cuc for episodic memory.
For example, regeneration memory would not provide an answer to: "I asked you for the name of a certain kind of famous person.
What kind of person was I asking for?" or "I asked you for a word starting with a letter.
Which letter was it?" Although we do not find in thc literature experiments that support directly the idea of regencration memory, we would likc to discuss some results that providc indirect cvidence for such a mechanism.
'T'hc first result is that subjccts "unconsciously" change thcir attitudes as a result of being asked to argue for an opposing view.
The change is unconscious in the sense that subjects don't report being aware of changing their attitudes and pcrccive thcmsclves as having had the samc attitudes cven before the experimentally induced argument (Bem & McConnel, 1970).

(The correlation bctwccn recall and current attitude is very high: .96 to .98.) Control subjccts without any expcrimcntal manipulation bchave as if they make two attempts to generate attitudes—one for the recall and one for the current attitudc.
We can also account for the finding that the subiccts who remcmbered the instruction to give cvidence against their prior attitude showed less attitude change.
(Thc nunber of subjects forgetting this component of the instructions was remarkably high.) Remembering the restriction might reflect memory of difficulty in suppressing counter-arguments that were accessed at the time for making the attitude judgment.
In an intcrcsting scrics of studics, Fischhoff (1975,1977) has demonstrated that being informed about the answer to a question or the outcome of a situation changes subjects' pcrccptions of how well they knew thc answer (knew-it-all-along cffcct), or how likcly they judged the outcomc of the situation to be (hindsight).

This reprocessing vicw can also account for Fischhoffs observation (1977) that subjects can "remember" or rcgencrate many of their original judgments an hour later, when thcy are not given additional information.
The subjects were instructed to remember thcir original responses, but wc don't know if the subjccts would havc been cqually accurate if they were simply askcd to answer the qucstion again (i.c., asked cxplicitly to reprocess the answer). Λ similar analysis can account for the surprising observation that training and trcatment will not change self-report mcasures taken prior and subscqucnt to trcatment, cven when objcctivc changes are demonstratcd (Howard, 1980).
