## Summary
Protocol analysis using gencral, task-indcpcndcnt process categories has not greatly extended our understanding of cognitive processes.
Those relations that have becn obtained, and which are not artifactual, are weak, accounting for only a small part of thc variability in performance.
Predictability is low even when the protocols arc collected for the same solutions from which performance mcasurcs were derivcd.
Ideally, we would collect protocol data from one sct of solution proccsses and make predictions for the performance of the same individuals on another set of solutions to different problems.
It would be crroncous to conclude from these negative results that there is no useful information to be extracted from the protocols.
The mcthods of analysis used in the studies describcd in this scction are different from thosc that we advocatc.
The processcs of gencrating data from the protocols also incorporate numerous assumptions, which may be invalid.
It is possible that the particular sets of general processes assumed in these studies are not the right ones.
Alternatively, it is possible that good problem solvers cannot be discriminated from poor ones by differcnces in such general, task-indepcndent processes.
Wc start with thc obvious obscrvation that if somcone lacks the knowledge necessary for performing a task, no number of gencral skills will save the day for him.
Expert and excellent performance in one domain does not predict the quality of performancc in another, unrclated domain.
In mathematics problem solving, Wcbb (1975) showcd that thc ovcrwhclmingly important and successful predictor was mathematical knowledge.
A study by Gimmestad (1977), relying csscntially on Kilpatrick's coding schemes, provides data that allow us to cxamine one of the assumptions about task-independent processes.
T’he assumption in question is that thc relation betwcen reliancc on heuristics and problemsolving pcrformancc should be the same for all problems, at least in a given problem cnvironment. Λnalyzing the relation bctween the number of instantiatcd heuristics on individual problems and pcrformance on those problems, she found that different heuristics were differentially useful for specific problems.
More important, she found that the use of certain heuristics was negatively corrclated with success on some problcms, and at least one of thc ncgativc rclations she dctectcd was statistically significant.
In order to cvaluate the consistency of subjccts' use of heuristics on very similar problems, she constructed two problems that called on the same algcbra but had different semantic content.
'Ihere was no indication that the subjects uscd the same heuristics on both problems.
Although it is clear from other research, for cxample Hayes and Simon (1976), that isomorphic problems are not ncccssarily perccived and representcd in the same way, this lack of consistency in the usc of heuristics raises questions about what is actually captured in these kinds of protocol encodings.
In sum, wc bclieve that at our current levcl of understanding, an analysis of thc hecded information rcvealed in a protocol, in the context of a task analysis, is a morc fruitful approach to protocol analysis of cognitive processcs than is an cncoding and analysis in terms of taskindependcnt gencral processes.

## VERBAL
REPORTS AND THEORIES Theories in psychology have usually becn formulated in highly abstract terms.
Many of them make predictions only for aggregated data that are pooled over items and over subjects.
Somc thcorics posit mechanisms that specify, on some level, how behavior is generated under different experimcntal conditions.
In this section, we wish to illustrate with a few examplcs the relevance and import of verbal reports for tcsting such theorics.
In the remaining chapters of this book we will be more concerned with how verbal reports can be used to generate and test detailed information processing models of task performance.
When verbal reports contradict theories that are not disconfirmed by other cxperimental data, it is convenicnt to disregard the reports as epiphenomcnal.
But, if we belicve that the verbal reports are pertinent, and not cpiphcnomcnal, we should show that a gcncral thcory adequately captures the verbal information on somc level of abstraction.
We will cvaluate various ways in which implications of thcorics can bc tested against thc detailed sequences of hecded information.
Wc will also point to cases where such tests lead to rejection of the corresponding theory.
Protocol data have bcen uscd to support and refute proposed mechanisms underlying various proccsscs.
Verbal reports, even from a small number of subjects, can serve as evidencc that at lcast some subjects' cognitive processes conform to a hypothesized model of the scquencc and type of information that is heeded.
In such situations the verbal reports serve as evidence for the cxistencc of ccrtain cognitive structures and processes, an important first step towards gaining evidence for generality and gencralizability.
Similarly, evidence of the existence of some cognitive structures in the mcmories of some subjccts can rcfute the universality of a theory that makes strong predicitions about the nature and range of internal cognitive states.
A sccond issuc is thc relation bctwecn the information-rich data on the course of cognitive proccsses, and mathcmatical models that posit general characteristics of processes.
Many assumptions in mathematical models of cognitive proccsses do not have to be left as assumptions, but can be converted into testable predictions on the level of process data.
A third and related issue has to do with ways of understanding, in terms of mediating processes, cmpirical relations between observed behavior and expcrimcntal manipulations.
'The first publishçd study using 'TΛ protocols was carried out by Watson (1920).
He instructcd one of his friends to think aloud while trying to identify the function of an unfamiliar physical object.
From his analysis of the protocol, Watson made two different theoretical points.
First, he showed that the problem solving bchavior could not be scen as insightful or as a sequence of logically connected steps.
'The vicw that problem solving was always driven by'a rational, delibcrativc process could thus be rejected.

It is when we ask him to think aloud ... that we begin to grasp how relatively crude is the process of thinking.
Here we see typified all of the errors made by the rat in the maze: false starts appear; emotional factors show themselves, such as the hanging of the head and possibly even blushing when a false scent is followed up.
'The subject returns again and again to his starting point as shown by his asking, "You say the given facts are so and so?" 'The experimenter says, "Yes," and again thc subject starts off.
(Watson, 1920, p.
91) However, Watson docs not make the mapping to trial-and-error processes any more explicit.

Dunckcr (1926, 1945) provides perhaps the best example of using protocol data to reject other thcories and in support of his own account.
Duncker presents a logical argument against the sufficiency of associative and S-R thcorics to account for productive problem solving (problem solving where the subjccts cannot rely on memory of cxpcricncc with identical or similar problems).

In testing their thcory of anagram problem solving against information in 'TΛ protocols, Mayzner, Tresselt and Helbock (1964) found that their theory could not account for many of the words heeded, cspecially words that contained letters not contained among those presented in the anagram.

Grudin (1980) showcd that subjects can and do vary their strategies in solving verbal analogics (i.c., Λ:B::C:?) beyond what was assumed in the cxisting thcories (Sternberg, 1977).

ITEM: BIRD:FISH:AIR: (BREATHE, SWIM, WATER) PROTOCOL: "bird is to fish (pause) birds are in air, fish are in (pause) water." (Grudin, 1980, p.
72) This protocol clearly contradicts the theory, in that the relation between Λ and C is found and applicd to B.

## CONCLUSION
Our main conccrn in this chapter has becn to investigatc the claim that has frcqucntly becn made that thinking-aloud protocols and other verbal reports are epiphenomenal, and cannot be rclied upon to provide cvidencc about the course of ongoing task pcrformancc.
We have asscmbled all of the expcrimcntal evidence wc could find that bcars on this issue.
With great consistency, this cvidencc demonstratcs that verbal data arc not in the least epiphenomenal but instcad are highly pertinent to and informative about subjects' cognitive processes and memory structures.
Human subjects arc not schizophrenic crcatures who produce a strcam of words, parallel but irrclevant to the cognitive task thcy are performing.
On the contrary, their thinking aloud protocols and retrospective reports can revcal in remarkable detail what information they arc attending to while performing their tasks, and by revealing this information, can provide an orderly picture of the cxact way in which the tasks are being performed: the strategics employed, thc inferences drawn from information, the acccssing of memory by recognition. ∧s we saw in the final scction of the chapter, verbal data often provides a powerful means for testing broad theorctical gencralizations, which can somctimes be confirncd or refuted by demonstration of the presence or absence of certain information in subjects' verbalizations.
But the real promise of verbal data, a promise alrcady partly realized over the past two or threc decades, lies in their use in developing and testing detailed information proccssing models of cognition, models that can often be formalized in computer programming languages and analyzcd by computer simulation.
'To take advantage of the powcr of verbal data in carrying out this enterprise, we must develop a mcthodology for cncoding and interpreting these data.
'The remaining chapters of this book are centrally concerncd with this methodology. # MODEL OF VERBALIZATION Up to this point, we have aimed mainly at identifying from verbalizations what information subjects attend to.
In this chapter, we will add to our model of verbalization more detail about the underlying processes, as a basis for our subsequent discussion of techniques of protocol analysis.
We will not alter our earlier general model, but will strengthen the assumptions on which it is based and add some new assumptions.
We will describe first, in summary form, the model for concurrent verbalization.

## GENERAL
MODEL AND ASSUMPTIONS The model of Chapter 2 showed the dependence of verbalizations on how information is stored and represented, and showed how verbalizations are coordinated with the ongoing cognitive processes.
The model allowed us to predict the existence and locus of effects of instructions for various kinds of verbalizing.
In this chapter, we will focus on the content of the verbalizations, and the relation of that content to the way in which information is represented internally.
The following assumptions are at the core of the model: 1.
The verbalizable cognitions can be described as states that correspond to the contents of STM (i.e., to the information that is in the focus of attention).
2.
The information vocalized is a verbal encoding of the information in short-term memory.
In order to be able to discuss in more detail how the contents of STM are verbalized, we need to find some way of describing the information structures it holds.
For lack of a better label, we will refer to them as thoughts.
Since only one thought can be verbalized at a time, we necd a mcchanism that determines which onc.
In addition, we want to specify how non-verbal thoughts are translated into verbal forim.
By understanding this translation process we should be better able to infer the non-verbal representations from the observed vocalizations.
'T'he first additional assumption we require is that thoughts are selected for verbalization as they are heeded.
3.
'The verbalization processes are initiated as a thought is heeded.
'The second assumption relates to structure.
4.
'The verbalization is a direct cncoding of the heeded thought and reflects its structure.
Up to this point, we have used the terms "talk aloud" and "think aloud" interchangcably.
In applying our more dctailed model, it wilt sonetiımnes be necessary to distinguish the case wlere a subject utters thoughts that are alreadv encoded in verbal form from the case where the subject recodes verbally and utters thoughts that may have been held in memory in some other form (e.g., visually).
When it is necessary to make the distinction, we will refer to these two forms of uterance as talking aloud and thinking aloud, respectively.
In providing protocols, subjects will not always distinguish betwcen these two kinds of verbalizations, but to some cxtent, differcnces in instructions (scc the Appendix to Chapter 7) may influcncc thcm to produce the one or the other.
The nature of the task will often have even more influcnce on the verbalizations.
When it is not clear which term better describes the verbalizations, wc will generally refer to them as "thinking aloud." Before we discuss the cognitive processes involved in verbalizing under talk-aloud or think-aloud instructions, we need to discuss briefly these cognitive structures that we are calling thoughts.

## Characterizing
Cognitive Structures ("Thoughts") We will have little to add to the long-standing argument over whether all mental content is verbal, or at least verbalizable (Sec McKcllar (1968) for such a discussion).
Holding to our carlier limits, we will only consider heeded information that is relevant for task-dirccted cognitive processes.
This restriction relieves us from considering many of the most controversial kinds of mental content.
The restriction to thoughts that reflect heeded information in STM means that the "stream of thought," discussed by James (1890), will not concern us.
According to James' own characterization thcsc peripheral elements are never completely hecded.
Likewise, day-drcanis and similar thoughts contain imagery that never is hecded directly.
We will also cxclude feclings fromn the thoughts we will consider Many of the categorics of thought wc are excluding raise difficult problems of interprctation and analysis.
'T’he difficulties are not nearly so grcat for task-relevant information acquired through verbal instructions and verbal problem stimuli.
In Chaptcr 3 we prescnted cmpirical evidence to show that the kinds of thoughts we are considcring are generally sufficient to account for the cognitive mechanisms in task performance.
In ncarly all linguistic analyses, the sentence is regarded as the verbal realization of a meaningful idca.
'Task-relevant informnation to which a subject attends, even if it is sometimes figural rather than verbal, can usually be described at least approximately in terms of propositions that are expressable in sentences. Λs our discussion of visual imagery in Chapter 2 suggests, however, the encoding of some kinds of stimulus information into sentences may be quite complex and difficult.
For the present, we will consider stimuli that do not present this difficulty.
How can wc use sentencc structure to discriminate bctwcen differcnt mental contexts in which information can bc hecded?
There are many different kinds of verbal information.
Some information reflects the current problem situation.
It may be an encoding of the stimulus, or information that is true of the task.
Verbalizations of this Current-State information arc often marked by vcrbs such as "be," "have," ctc., in the present tense.
Soine verbalizations reflect intentions or goals to attain configurations or attributes not true for the current situation.
'This Future-State information is often marked by verbs or verb constructions like "want to havc," "likc to havc," or verbs in the futurc tense.
Finally, soimne informnation in verbalizations is modal in character.
Modal-State information is hypothctical or conjectural, and verbalizations of this type are marked by "if..." constructions or verbs likc "assume," "guess," or constructions involving "maybe" or "pcrhaps." We scc that the primary cucs for identifying thesc different kinds of thoughts are thc verbs and their tenses.
Occasionally finer distinctions in the underlying processes are made: "I remcmbered that...," "] noticed that...," "I forgot that...." These implicit descriptions of the processes will be discussed in more detail later.

When subjects are recalling thoughts from memory or percciving information in the environment, thoughts can be heeded much faster than they can possibly be verbalizcd.
We will deal with the resulting incompletencss in a spccial section in this chapter.
Here we will focus on verbalization of more complex thoughts and the effects of context on the form of the verbalizations. l.ct us first look at effects of context and perspcctivc.
Context can be induced by presenting events in a particular order.
Osgood (1971) demonstrated that the form and content of verbali/ed descriptions of stimulus events reflected the structure of the perceptual situation and the subjects' presuppositions bascd on cvents presented previously.
The extent to which objects were perceivcd as ncw or previously sccn was dircctly linked to the use of indefinitc or dcfinite deterniners and pronouns.

In a controlled cxpcriment, Jcrcmy (1978) found that whether events occurred at the samne or different times, or the same or different locations affected the structure of verbalizations about the events, but the content of the events produced no effect.
In an interesting study of subjects attempts to comprehend the mcchanisms of sewing machines, Miyake (1982) showcd that thc 'mental" points of view of subjects could be assessed from their verbalizations.
She showed that there was a relation betwcen shifts in point of view and lack of understanding and that final understanding was associated with a stable point of vicw.
The point of vicw was assessed through occurrences of verbs, like "go" and "come," and demonstratives, like "this" and "here." Λ view from above the scwing machine was, for example, inferred from verbalizations dcscribing the nccdle as "going down" and "comes up." Conversely, a view from below was inferred by describing the needle as "comes down" and "goes up." 742).
We postulate that verbalization of complex recalled thoughts is in many ways similar to verbalization of new sequences of thoughts.
Because of the limits of STM capacity, complex thoughts are not kept as entities in STM. Λ complex thought can bc hecded as a whole only in the scnsc that all the subordinate clcments arc directly available for retrieval and subscquent attention.

(Simon & Barenfeld, 1969).

## Verbalizing
Cognitive Process In the prcvious sections of this chapter we were primarily concerned with verbalization of hecded information.
'This information is both the output of processing and the input to subsequent processing.
For our purposes we can vicw the attention to new inforination as instantancous.
Since cognitive processes have a nonncgligible duration, our inference that we are attending to them derives from our awareness of a sequence of internal states.
'T’he information heeded during the exccution of a process is our only source of data about the structure of that process.
In this section our aimn is two-fold.
First, wc will specify how descriptions of cognitive activities can bc gencrated within our model.
Second, we will specify under what circumnstances such dcscriptions are verbalizcd and when they becomc an obtrusive activity induced by instructions to verbalize.
We would like to discriminate threc different sources of information that would allow subjects to report on activities with duration.
First, in many situations the cognitive activity has an external counterpart in motor activitics, which can cither be observed visually or by means of other inforation available in the sensory stores.
Second, due to the limited capacity of STM, information will only reside there for a limited time and it is possible that subjccts have information about this time in STM.
'Third, higher-level activities like rcading and writing are made up of nuncrous subprocesses that usc SlM ·for inputs and outputs.
Subjects' awarencss of these inputs and outputs enables them to report the occurrence and duration of the higher-level activitics.
As processes become automated, less and less information becomes available about them.
T’his is particularly truc of many motor activities.
Tasks involving physical manipulation do not producc detailed verbal traces of thc motor activity.
What arc verbalized in these situations are the higher-level dircctions for the manipulative attempts (Ruger, 1910) and monitoring cvaluations of the sucess of attempts (Klinger, 1974).
Evcn though this may be the usual casc, still the subject can change his processing and describe the activity in detail from his pcrception of his own visual, kincstetic or tactile input.
Examples of this kind of verbalization of motor and perceptual-motor activitics are given by McNeill (1975).
He asked subjects to describe cach movement as they made it in highly autoıatized activities, like sitting down on the floor and rising to standing, and in other tasks, like assembling an aquariuımn.
By analyzing the vidcotape recordings, he found a very close temporal correspondence betwcen the movements and the verbal descriptions.
In the assembly task the verbal description was initiated after the motor activity was initiated, suggesting that the verbal description was cucd by the motor process.
In the highly automatic activities there was an almost perfect correspondence between the initiation of the verbal description and the movement, suggesting that the anticipated next movement served as a cue for the verbal description.
Although subjects are able to access and attend to motor processes and also describe them, in most cases this is an additional activity unrelated to the verbalization of the information heeded in the normal course of the process.
For many motor skills the verbalization is highly obtrusive.
Although the instruction to "think aloud" clearly asks for verbalization of heeded information, it soinctimes evokes descriptions of activities instcad.

'The subject in the example above spoke less than 40 words/minute.
Wc would not bc safe in cxtrapolating to this kind of verbalization thc conclusions wc have rcachcd about think-aloud protocols that report mainly STM contents.
Verbalization of activities may possibly influcnce the problem solving process, although we are not awarc of specific cvidcncc that it does.
Although we consider the process of attention or heeding as essentially instantancous, it may be possible to determine how long a given picce of information is retained in STM.
Information about future states, given premises, goals or subgoals will bc kept in STM as long as they actually direct the subjects' processing. lt is therefore understandable why subjects use the present progressive in the following type of construction: "Now I am thinking that I shall gct 1 up therc" (Fricsson, 1975b, p.
93) Sirilarly for modal states in planning: "And knowing that the two I.'s add up to some numbcr greater than 10" (Ncwell & Simon, 1972, p.
264) These kinds of verbalizations are derived from information that is heeded, but they are generated as responses to a probe, like "What am I thinking about?", and not dircctly as reports of the information attended to.
Cognitive activities of the third type are organized into skills that are used recurrently.
If the skills are highly automated, reportable intermediate states may occur infrcquently; otherwise, the attempt to report the activity may compete for processing capacity with verbal cncoding processes.
Examples of such activities are reading simple text, doing arithmetic, scarching visually for displayed information, recalling information from mciory, gencrating combinations by manipulation.
When such activitics are cxecuted, subjects may refer verbally to the activity and its associated goal at the time the activity is initially heeded (e.g., "I.et me see if I can reimember how I did it last time.").
The activities mentioned can be of high or low level, broad or narrow scope: "I want to solve this problem first," or "I want to find the value of Y first." Items seem most likely to be mentioned when the decision is being reached to take them up next, rather than while the activity is actually under way.
As subjects acquire more skill in a domain through practice, they develop a more sophisticated internal representation and better methods for attaining goals.
Subjects may both attend to these proccdures and plans, and also verbalize them.
Initially a subject may recognize that he can apply a procedure he has used at an carlier time.
Later he may simply refer to it as "the procedure for attaining X." Such a report is differcnt from a rcference to a procedure as it is heeded. Λ subject can only report that he has used a procedure previously if he can recall some of the carlicr instances.
Hence, such a report suffers all of the deficicncies of recall from l.l'M, and must bc interprcted more cautiously than a report of information that is being heeded.

Between Verbal Reports and Descriptions A few studics address dircctly thc differcnccs between thinking aloud and various kinds of descriptions.

## INCOMPLETE
VERBALIZATION OF INFORMATION IN STM We return now to the issue of the completeness of verbalizations, first discussed in Chapter 3.
The central problem is that thought in non-oral form can procced much faster than spcech.
Thc major cmpirical evidence for the incompleteness of information in think-aloud protocols is twofold: (1) inconsistency in how much is reported on repctitions of esscntially the samc proccss, and (2) comparisons of think-aloud protocols with retrospective reports.
When a thought structure comes into attention, it serves at the same time as the input to the processes for verbalization.

Earlier, we reviewed the cvidence that these processes overlap in time.

Where the task is an unfamiliar onc, the problem may not arise, since new information comes into attention at a slow pace.
We will focus on situations where expericnce and skill in the task permit information to bc acquircd rapidly.
In these situations, a number of difficultics arise in trying to slow down the cognitive processes without changing them.
First, it is hard to control the very rapid processes that acquire new information by recognition.
When, for example, a subject is scanning a visual stimulus for information and recognizes something, it may be impossible for him to prevent himself from rccognizing additional structures before he has reported the first onc—unless the visual stimulus can be removed at the moment of the initial recognition.
This difficulty is likely to arise, for example, for subjects in the anagram task who adopt the simple strategy of acquiring information by recognition until sufficient cues have been obtained to clicit the word from memory.
Second, some cognitive processes can only be executed under time constraints.
'There are many cases, especially in the motor domain, where processes cannot be slowed down without drastically changing outcome and accuracy.
Examples of such activities are juggling and riding a bicycle.
'There are also activitics where the rapid decay of sensory stores imposes bounds on the time during which the information in those stores can bc accessed.
Interruption and suppression of rehcarsal lead to a rapid loss of information from STM.
Hence, wc. would expcct that prolonged attention to items in ST'M to allow verbalization will be disruptive of tasks that impose high loads on SI'M.
To assess how serious these problems of verbalization are, we need to examinc thc relevant cınpirical cvidcncc.

## Techniques
for Increasing Verbalization Several experimental techniqucs may be used to incrcasc concurrent verbalization.
In terms of our model, we can describe thesc techniques as being aimed at slowing down the task-dirccted proccsses.

Wc have found studics using at least four different techniqucs to secure more complete reporting: 1.
Perccptual access to the stimulus may be denied.
Then subjects have to generate new states internally, and cannot rely on rapid recognition of changing stimulus characteristics.
We have alrcady discussed studics using this techniquc (Benjaficld, 1971; Durkin, 1937).
A more cxtreme method is to replace the cxternal stimulus by information that must be held internally (c.g., mental multiplication, addition, and paperfoldiņg tasks).
2.
Stimuli may be segmented into smaller picces of information that are prescnted at a slower rate.
Well-known examples arc the use of information-displays in dccision-making, where the subjects are shown a matrix of information with alternatives and attributes as dimensions.
The values are not pcrccptually available, but can be accessed cither by turning over cards or by requcsting the information from the experimenter.
(For a review and discussion of such methodology, see Lehmann & Moore (1980) and Payne, Braunstcin, & Carroll (1978).) Below wc will discuss in more detail some cxamples from reading studics where the tcxt is broken up into a scqucncc of physically separated sentences to break the flow of perceptually based recognition.
3.
Ongoing skilled activitics may be interrupted with a signal to givc a report of the contents of attention.
In many skilled activitics, like piano-playing, typing, and other skills where real-time performnance is an intcgral part of the skill, attempts to slow down the cognitive processes may altcr thcım grcatly.

Reminders to Think Aloud.
When subjccts think aloud they are doing somcthing more than they normally do while thinking.
'They are, at least, ovcrtly vocalizing their verbal thoughts and, in addition, encoding non-verbal thoughts into verbal form.
Although subjccts require very little instruction to enable them to think aloud, most pcople's normal modc of thinking is silent.
Even after tens of hours of producing protocols, subjects never complain that they are unable to revert to their customary silent thinking. !n order to account for the subjects' ability to think aloud in cxperiments, we have to assume that 'T'Λ processes are controlled by a marker in STM.
For tasks involving non-vcrbal information, task-rclevant information can be accessed fastcr than it can be cncodcd and vocalized.
Whcn task-relevant processes rcquire a lot of STM capacity, subjects often stop verbalizing (luncker, 1945; Johnson, 1964) and remain silent.
However, even a brief reminder from the experimcnter will start them speaking again.
'These remindcrs may take many forms like, "Pleasc, tell me what you are thinking," "Plcasc, think aloud," "Kcep talking," etc.
Wc would rccommend "Kcep talking" because it is the least dircctive and does not require any direct answer to the experimenter.
Our interpretation of these phenomena is that the marker in STM directing the verbalization of thoughts may disappcar when task-relevant information is being accessed rapidly.
'The simple reminder reinstates the marker.
In fact, the reminder does not have to be verbal, for tones appcar to serve just as well.
In support of the vicw that, during intervals of silencc, thoughts are hecded but not verbalized, wc find that subjects will almost invariably resume reporting in response to reminders to think-aloud (Ericsson, 1975b).
Occasionally, howcver, subjccts will report that they are not attending to any thoughts and that their minds arc "blank." In our experience it is important to have subjects do warm-up tasks with oral information (See Appendix.).
'T’his appcars to climinate silence due to misunderstanding of the instruction to think aloud.
It gives subjects practice in expressing thoughts dircctly without explaining or interrelating the information.
According to our model the information reported in response to a reminder should be the same as the information reported spontancously, with one important difference.
When subjects are verbalizing concurrently, they will verbalize the information as it is hecdcd.
However, when subjects have becn remindcd to think aloud, they will verbalize the information in ST'M.
But not all information resides in STM for the saimne length of time. Λlmost any model of the cognitive processes would prcdict that goals will be kept in STM longer (usually, until they are satisficd) than intermcdiate results, which can be discarded as soon as they have been used as imputs for subscquent proccssing.
'Thus, our model would predict a relatively high frequcncy of reports of goals in response to reminders.
In a study by Ericsson (1975b), the verbalized information was sorted into several gencral categories, that are described in Chapter 4. lmmcdiately after reminders, goals and intentions were verbalized relatively more frequently, as compared with recognitions of relations and evaluations, than in other portions of the protocols.

## IMPLICATIONS
FOR PROTOCOL ANALYSIS 'The basic assumption of our model is that the information in focal attention is vocalized directly ( in the case of an oral cncoding ) or vocalized after an initial encoding into oral verbal code.
The obvious implication of this for analyzing rccorded verbalizations is that thc originally hecded information should be recovered by decoding the "encoded" verbalizations (i.c. those not originally in oral form).
'The first step in such an analysis is to identify the verbalization units (segments) that correspond to units of heeded information.
If verbalizations reflect the internal representation, we can usc syntactic information as well as pauses in articulation, phonemic intonation contours, and stress to uncover these units.
The second implication of the model is that cach segment is verbalized independently of those that prccede and follow it; hence that each can be encoded independently, without attention to context.
This independence of protocol segments from context is incomplete in several respccts.
First of all. pronouns and descriptive phrases can often only be interpreted in the context of the preceding verbalizations.
In most cases, the rcferenced entity can be casily identificd and substituted in a pre-coding stage.
'There will, of course, be more difficult cases, where information is heirarchically organized, and the structure of contexts complex.
A third implication of our model is that verbalizations should be encoded in terms of the heeded information they express.
'Thinking aloud protocols consist almost entirely of verbalizations of hecded information. Λt the current state of our knowledge, other types of verbalizations contained in them (c.g., descriptions of process) present a more complex coding task.
For example: "I remcmbcred that last time I tricd to substitute ..." Fictional An appropriate infercnce from this segment is that the subject is attending to his memory for carlier goal-driven activities that he now recalls performing.
Because of the possibility of error in recall from LTM, it is incorrect to infer that he actually' performed them carlier.
This last point is very important, and highlights a diffcrence between some common practices of protocol analysis and the practices our model would recominend.
Many procedures attempt to encode the processes that gencrate heeded information, rather than the information itself.
But the processes can only be implicd from thc information in ST'M, which does not, as wc have secn, usually includc information about process.
Information can be brought to the attention of the subject in many different ways.
It can be retrieved from L'T'M, or it can simply be recognized and detected as part of the perceptually available stimulus display.
Or it can be the product of somc process, inferential or other.
Currently, we don't know cnough about thc structure and form of verbalizations to bc certain that thcy contain cucs that would enable us to distinguish different historics of generation.
Encoding the occurrence of a specific process on the basis of protocol data requires assumptions about the underlying mechanisimns.
Hcncc it is more in the nature of a thcoretical cxplanation than a simple encoding of data.
In a later chapter, we will discuss the relations among raw data, interpreted data, and theory. # METHODS FOR PROTOCOL ANALYSIS Having devcloped and examined in dctail a model of the way in which verbal reports are gencrated, we are now ready to discuss spccific techniques for deriving valid data from them.
First we will describe a number of specific methods of analysis that have been used, and then we will examine them in the light of the methodological principles that should govern the encoding of verbal protocols.

## EARLY
PROTOCOL ANALYSIS In carly work, protocols of subjects thinking aloud consistcd of the cxperimenters' notes summarizing the vocalizations rather than direct transcriptions of the subjects' actual words.
Until tape recorders bccame available (about 1945), therc were no practicable means to record verbalizations.
Thc investigator was forced to sclect and interpret the subject's specch in real time, without any chance of going back to reinterpret or reevaluate the initial records and encodings.
The carlicst documcnted analysis of a think-aloud protocol of which we arc awarc was made by Watson (1920). Λs we saw in Chapter 4, he used the protocol to illustrate some gencral characteristics of cognitive process in problem solving, presenting his own interpretation and description of the protocol with little or no effort to providc systematic cvidence in support of his vicws.
Subscquent rescarch using protocol analysis attcmptcd to take down thc idcas morc closely as they were gcncratcd by thc subjcct.
Duncker (1926) analyzcd a numbcr of protocols for over 20 problems in search of the mechanisms that gencrated the solutions.
His analysis (Duncker, 1926, 1945) was a metalevcl description of the solution attempts and thcorctical mechanisms that could gencrate the transitions to new ideas for possible solutions.
Scyeral studies (Bulbrook, 1932; Durkin, 1937) set out to find the nature of insights and the conditions under which they occur.
From their analyses of protocols, they contended that the observed processes did not imply any special phenomenon of insight but could be described in terms of other kinds of cognitive processes.
De Groot (1965) recorded extensive 'TΛ protocols of chess players selecting moves in games, and used the theoretical framework proposed by Otto Sclz (1913) to cncode the processes he found expressed in them.
While the protocols were recorded by hand, and hence certainly incomplete, they contained enough information to allow de Groot to draw a rather detailed picture of the problem-solving processes of novice and expert chess players.
He was generally able to reconstruct the subjects scarch trees, and provide examples from the protocols of the processes postulated by Selz.
The outstanding fcature of most of this carly work is its cxploratory nature.
'T'hc main aim was to gencratc conccpts and potential mechanisms rather than to address questions of validation and generality.
The contact between the protocols and the theoretical ideas was through the investigators' descriptions and interpretations of the protocols, which had to be gencrated in real time.
T’here could be little explicit, detailed comparison betwcen theory and thc protocol record.
Many methodological issues simply could not be addressed when the subjects original verbalizations could not be preserved in their raw form.
With the introduction of tape recorders after World War Il, the situation changed markedly, for it was now possible to analyze the verbalizations without any real time constraints.
The practice of transcribing the tapes litcrally into typewritten form devclopcd rapidly.
From written transcripts. the investigator could obtain almost instant access to all the verbalizations corresponding to a given process.
Issues of coding reliability could also be addressed by presenting several coders with the same raw transcript of the verbalizations.
With the cmergencc of computer simulation of cognitive processes (Ncwell & Simon, 1956; Newcll & Shaw, 1957) modcls were proposed that made cxplicit claims as to what information was processed by subjects, hence could become part of the verbal protocol.
Intensive analysis was made of a small number of verbal protocols for a task, sometimes a single protocol, to demonstrate that the information in the protocol could be regenerated, approximately, by the simulation model opcrating on the same task.
Wc will have a good dcal to say about this approach in this chapter.
In Chapter 4, we have already discussed another strcam of literature, in which information in verbal protocols has been encoded at a very abstract level with the aim of uncovering generalizable aspects of cognitive processes.
As we saw there, the majority of these studies did not test specific hypotheses or models of the cognitive processes but sought to induce and identify regularitics and patterns in the recorded data.
In many of these studies, the protocol data were cncoded into very general categorics, and these categories were related only weakly to any process description of cognitive processes capable of performing the tasks.
'The link between protocol and encoding was often not cxplicit, and it was often not clear on what basis the encoding decisions were reached.
We will not pay much further attention to these methods in this chapter.

## INTRODUCTION
TO TECHNIQUES OF PROTOCOL ANALYSIS In this section we describe some forms of protocol analysis that are especially useful for comparing sequences of verbal bchavior with the bchavior predicted by models expressed as computer programs.
'These methods retain, as fully as possible, the content of the protocol (low-level encoding), so as to permit very detailed matching of the encodings with the trace of the program.

## Basic
Assumptions 'The methods to be described are not theoretically neutral; they rest on a sct of assumptions about thc gcneral structure of problem-solving proccsses, and about the verbal reporting process itself.
The major theorctical assumptions that underlie these methods are: 1.'Thc subjcct's bchavior can bc viewed as a scarch through a problem space, accumulating knowledge (not always correct) about thc problem situation as hc goes.
This gradual, step-by-step accumulation of knowledge can be rcpresented by a problem behavior graph, the kth nodc of which rcpresents the subjcct's knowledge after k steps of search.
2.
Each step in the scarch involves the application of an operator, sclected from a rclatively small sct of task-rclcvant operators, to knowlcdgc hcld by thc subjcct in STM. Λpplication of the opcrator brings ncw knowledge into STM, moving thc subject to a new point in the problem space.
3.
'The verbalizations of the subject correspond to some part of the information he is currently holding in STM, and usually to information that has recently been acquired.
4.'The information in STM, and reported by the subject, consists primarily of knowledge required as inputs to the operators, new knowledge produced by operators, and syımbols representing active goals and subgoals that are driving the activity. Λ goal may take the form of an intent to apply an opcrator; in which case the protocol may contain explicit evidence for the application of operators.
The first two of thcse four assumptions can be vicwed as weak postulates about the problem-solving process (wcak because a wide range of alternative processes can be represented as searches).
The third and fourth assumptions do little more than summarize the postulates about verbalization that we have been using throughout this book.
Therefore, they do not introduce important new assumptions into the protocol analysis process.

## Encoding
Vocabulary As a preliminary to the cncoding process, the task and the protocol are analyzcd to cxtract the vocabulary of objccts and rclations nccded to define the problem space and operators.
For·example, in the Tower of Hanoi task, a subjcct might refer in his protocol to "disks" and "pegs," and to "moving lisk X from Peg Y to Peg Z." essentially using the language of the problem instructions.
(See the protocol reproduced as an appcndix to Λnzai and Simon, 1979.) Thc subject may identify the disks by numbers (l)isk 1 for the smallest, say), and thc pegs by letters (∆, B, C, from left to right).
'The labels may bc borrowed from the problem instructions, or devised by the subject.
To describe problem situations, the subject may use rclations like "larger" and "smaller," and more complex rclational naming devices like, "the ncxt smallest disk to Disk 2 on Peg Λ." Protocols almost always also contain information that reveals the subject's control and evaluative processes and goals.
For cxample, the protocol mentioned above contains such stateimnents as: "Oh it's getting therc," "this time it's casy," "I don't know for sure," "wrong," "5 will have to go to C," "l will move the remaining four from B to C." (The lattcr two statements represent goals because the indicated actions require multiple moves.) Synonyms.
At this point, ccrtain cquivalents may bc defined, to permit the protocol to be encoded in a simpler, canonical form.
For example, "smallest disk" may be defincd as synonymous with Disk 1, so that the former name may always be replaced by the latter in the encoded protocol.

Nevertheless, replacing terms by synonyms, even through reliably, may lose semantic content.

Completeness of Vocabulary.
The protocol may now be scanned to discovcr what statcments cannot bc coded in thc language thus far dcfincd.
Additional terms (c.g., goal expressions) may bc added to the list until as much of the protocol language as desired has been accounted for.
Experience shows that, for relatively well-structured problem solving tasks, a small vocabulary (in thc dozcns and hundreds, not thousands) of terms, relations, and statement forms is sufficient to code more than ninety pcr cent of the language of a protocol.
For example, the Tower of Hanoi protocol we have mentioned is about 2,000 words in length, but contains a vocabulary of only about 165 different words.
A good rule of thumb for protocols of any considerable length is that the number of different words will be betwcen five and ten per cent of the length of thc tcxt.
Usually thc different words will bc distributed by frequcncy in a highly skcwed way, following thc rank-frequency law of Zipf (1949) and Yule (1924).

The Use of Context.
'l'he use of context in coding protocols involves a tradcoff.
On the one hand, interpreting protocol statements in terms of context permits a much larger part of the semantic content of the protocol to be retained than if context is ignored.
On the other hand, when context is uscd in interpretation, thc cvidencc provided by each statement is no longer wholly independent of the evidence drawn from other statements (used to interpret the former).
We will have more to say about this issue presently.
The extent to which a particular mode of coding requircs consideration of context can also be illustrated by the protocol on the Tower of H-anoi problem reported by Anzai and Simon (1979).
The subject was making the actual moves in the problem on a large wooden Tower of Hanoi.
She verbalized every move, without exception, and in relatively uniform language.
She also verbalized soine of her goals, and some of the planning calculations that derived the ncxt move from the current goal.
A particularly clear passage from the beginning of her third trial of the problem is this one: 110.
If it were five, of course, 5 will have to go to C, right?
111.
So, 4 will be at B.
112.
3 will be at C.
113.
2 will be at B.
114.
So 1 will go from A to C.
This is the beginning of a new triai, where Disk 5 cannot legally be moved.
The situation, and the language (the conditional "if it were" and the "will have to") allow us to interpret statement l10 as describing a goal (G), and to encode it: (G:5 → C).
Since Disks 4, 3, and 2 also cannot be moved in this situation, and because of the "so" in 111, statements 111-113 are to be interpreted as a plan (P) for moves preparatory to moving Disk 5.

(M:1→C), and actually makes this move.

## Automation
of Encoding To incrcase the reliability and validity of encoding, various efforts can be made to automate the cncoding process.
We will mention two such systems here, PΛS and SΛPΛ.
Both will be discussed in more detail later in the chapter.
The most ambitious steps in this direction were taken by Newell and Waterman (1971, 1973) with the PΛS-1 and PΛS-II systems. Λ less ambitious attempt at moving toward automation of coding is the SΛPΛ (semi-automated protocol analysis) system of Bhaskar and Simon (1977).
While the PΛS systems, after the problem space has been defined and the protocol segmented manually, analyze the protocol automatically, to producc a problem bchavior graph, SΛPΛ is an intcractive program, spccially tailorcd to cach task environment, that supports the human coder in analyzing successive protocol segments.
A major advantage of automatic encoding is that it requires all of the underlying assumptions, the vocabulary and the inference rules, to be defined cxplicitly and applicd consistently.
Hencc, it makes clear exactly what assumptions have entered into the encoding.
Reliability is perfect (given thc samc protocol, thc systcm will always reach the same intcrpretation), and the robustness of the cncoding to changes in the underlying vocabulary and rules can be tested dircctly.
The loop is completed by testing the encoded protocol against the trace of a computer program that purports to provide a theory of the subject's behavior.
'Trace and protocol can be expressed in precisely the same formal language, so that there is nothing problematic about the comparison.
Notice that the test is really simultancously a test of the mutual consistency of the problem space definitions, the inference rules for encoding, and the theory of the subject's behavior.
Misfits between protocol and trace may be attributable to any of these sources.
This is exactly the situation we encounter in any theory testing, wherc a failure of data to fit theory perfectly may be duc to errors of observation, of instrunent calibration, of approximation (if wc lcave "unimportant" variables out of the theory), of incorrect auxiliary hypotheses (c.g., incorrect hypotheses about the operation of instruments), or of the theory itself.
What we are always testing, when wc confront a theory with data, is the mutual consistency of all of the presuppositions (including the theory itself) that underlie the comnparison.
Semi-automated protocol analysis does not remove all of the clements of subjcctivity that a completely automated proccdure does.
However, cxperiments with semi-automatic protocol analysis using SΛPΛ shows: (a) that it cnhances thc reliability with which coding can bc carried out; (b) that at lcast in tasks having fairly dcfinite structure imposed by the task cnvironment, the assumptions built into the program do not significantly distort the cncoding; and (c) that it makes the task considerably casier for the human coder.
Readers who have had actual expericnce in encoding verbal protocols will not underestimate the importance of this last point.
In particular, by focussing the coder's attention on individual segments, onc at a timc, and cucing possible interprctations, an interactive system for protocol analysis permits sustained attention to the coding task over much longer stretches of time than are tolerable without it.

## Level
of Analysis 'The kind of statcment-by-statement encoding we have been discussing so far retains most of the semantic content of the protocol.
For many purposes this is desirablc, or even indispensable.

What are some of the ways in which such aggrcgation can be accomplished?
Aggregation by Episodes.
For the description of problem-solving protocols at an aggregate level, Newell and Simon (1972) introduced the notion of problemn-solving episodes.
Certain steps in solving a particular problem may bc "obvious," other steps problematic.
For example, solving a problem in physics may involve writing down the appropriate algebraic cquation, then solving it.
If the cquation is simple and the subject skilled in algcbra, solving the cquation, oncc discovered, may be non-problematic, to be summarized as a single step in the problem behavior graph.
The detail of the solution may be of no particular interest from a problem solving standpoint beyond demonstrating that the subject has mastered the basic algorithms of algebra.
Gcneralizing from this cxamplc, a subject often organizes his problem solving efforts in terms of a hierarchy of subgoals.
Once this hierarchy has been identified, the protocol can be condensed, working in bottom-up fashion, by collapsing into a single step the segment of the protocol that relates to thc achicvement of a non-problematic subgoal—one that is reached by use of a well-practiced proccdure.
'T'he process that achieves the goal may be regarded as a macro-operator.
For example, a subject skilled in algebra may have a well-practiced procedure for solving lincar algebraic cquations in one unknown, so that the details of his solution process afford him no difficulty and are of no psychological interest.
In that case, "solve lincar cquation" can be cncoded as a single macro-operator that takes the subjcct to the new knowledge state containing the solution of the cquation.
An application of the cpisoding technique to the analysis of cryptarithinctic protocols at a rclatively abstract level may be found in Newell and Simon (1972), pp.
282-309.
Here the aggregated protocols revcaled very clcarly the differences among the problem spaces in which different subjects were working, and how these differences in problem spaces affected the way in which subjccts accumulatcd knowledge as they worked through the problem behavior graph.
The episodes also revealed clearly the common mcans-ends analysis heuristic that almost all of the subjects were using to organize thcir efforts.
Aggregation by Solution Steps.
In a study comparing the problcmsolving processes of cxperts and novices solving kincmatics probleins in physics, a similar summarizing technique was uscd to contrast the working-forward solution paths of the cxperts with the workingbackward solution paths of the novices (Simon & Simon, 1978).
This difference could be extracted objectively and reliably from thc protocols by recording as an cquation cach evocation of a principle of physics and its instantiation in terms of the data of the problem For cxample, "If the average speed was 200 meters per sccond, and the barrel is half a meter, .. then it would have to be 1/400 of a second," could be coded as: $$ 1 / \mathrm { V ^ { * } } = \mathrm { T } \left( .
5 / 2 0 0 = 1 / 4 0 0 \right) $$ where I, is length, $\mathrm { V } ^ { \star }$ is average velocity, and 'T' is time.
'Then cach protocol can be encoded in terms of the sequence of equations cach subjcct cvoked and instantiated, and thesc scqucnces can be compared betwcen subjects.
Aggregation by Processes.
Somctimes a number of consccutive protocol segments refer to the execution of a single major process by the subject, and this whole set can be given a single encoding.
For example, a major process in the cryptarithmctic task is to process a column, taking known information and substituting it for letters in the column in order to derive information about other letters.
"Each D) is 5; therefore, 'T' is zero" —obtained by processing the column that reads: D+D)=T.
The principal information that is verbalized by subjccts when proccssing a column is the identity of the column being processed, the information alrcady available about it (input information), and the new informnation derived (output information).

In 36 scgments each of which was an instancc of PC, thc numbcr of thc column bcing attendcd to was mentioned 34 times.
Some 37 input quantitics werc mentioned, and 21 omittcd; 43 output quantitics were mentioned, and 5 omitted.
In four cases where a contradiction was cncountered, ncither input nor output quantities were mentioned.

R, or E, all of which had remained constant for some time.
Of the 5 unmentioned outputs, 4 were carries.
Hencc, by coding cach instance of PC as a single segment, and without using any context outside that segment, almost completc information could bc obtained from the protocol about the information to which the subject had to attend in order to carry out the process and use its result.
Individual Differences.
As the cxamples cited show, aggrcgating protocols is an effective techniquc for studying individual differences different subjects.
It also suggests a comment on the common complaint that descriptions of problem solving gleaned from protocols cannot be gencralized.
The difficulties of gencralizing about problem solving from data obtained from individual protocols are not to be regarded simply as annoyances associated with the mcthod of protocol analysis.
The varicty in problem-solving processes is a psychological fact: Human beings differ widely in the knowledge thcy possess and the knowledge thcy cvoke and apply in particular problem-solving situations.
"Smcaring over" these genuine individual differences by aggregating data docs not destroy their reality; what it destroys is a large part of the information contained in the original data.
If human beings use different strategies in solving the same problem, wc cannot validate laws of behavior that assume the strategies to be all the samne.
Psychological invariants must be consistent with, and not dismissive of, this variety in human behavior.

## METHODOLOGICAL
ISSUES In scientific work we would like to separate "facts" from the theories that might be gencrated to explain or account for them.
The term data is usually used to denotc the factual information cmploycd for tcsting thcories.
According to thc conventional wisdom, data, properly gathered, must be acccpted by all scientists; theorics need not be, for the same data might bc explained in scveral different ways.
But matters are not quite so simple.
We have already sccn that various sorts of thcorctical commitments must bc made in the process of gathcring and recording data, and all data arc consequcntly tainted by thcory.
For example, theory-bascd decisions must bc madc as to what kinds of data are rclevant, hencc worth gathcring.
Obscrvations arc made with instruments, which are designcd on the basis of theory.
In these and other ways, theory crceps into the gathering and recording of data.
Still, wc wish to preserve the greatest possible distance bctween data and theory, so that data can be uscd to test theorics with a minimum of bias, pro or con, from preconceptions.
What wc must strive for is a kind of bootstrap operation.
In designing our data-gathcring schemnes, we make minimal essential theoretical commitments, then try to use the data to test stronger theories.
In fact, that is thc strategy wc have followed in this volume with respect to our theory of protocol analysis.
On the basis of weak assumptions about short-term memory, we were able to interpret the available experimental data on verbalization, to check whether these wcak assumptions are tenablc, and to strengthen them into a more complete theory of the verbalization process.

## Translating
Behavior Into Data Coombs (1964) has discussed the interdependence of theory and data in an illuminating way, and has analyzed how the observable aspects of psychological phenomena can be converted into data.
'The sequence of operations he describes for deriving data from traditional psychological measurements is fully parallel to the scquence for deriving data from recordings of verbal behavior.
Coombs (1964) starts thec cycle with a theory that already exists prior to any collection of observations.
'The theory delimits which aspccts of of potential observations should be recorded and become available for further processing.
Potential observations outside the limits will simply be ignored.
Coombs describes what might bc called thcory-driven science.
Scientific inquiry may also bc driven by data.
'l'hcory should not preclude the scientist from searching for new phenomena, or from paying serious attention to phenomena hc hits on adventitiously.
Many important scicntific discoveries have becn made in this way, with little prior guidance or disciplinc from theory.
As a second step, the observations that have been recorded are mapped onto the language of the theory.
If thc theory is sufficicntly wcak, it will allow the cxpression of altcrnative hypotheses (alternative strong subthcories).
We will use the term "data" to refer to the result of this mapping process, which encodes raw observations in the language of theory.
It is not hard to describe the corresponding steps in analyzing verbalizations.
When a tape recorder or vidco recorder is used to capture bchavior, a grcat dcal of information about thc subject is irretricvably lost (c.g., his blood pressure, EEG pattern, and many other potentially observablc phenomena).
'Transcribing rccorded tapes involves a further sclection of information, for the voicc inflections, for cxample, are usually ignored, or imperfectly encoded in punctuation.
'T’he more difficult problems arise, howcver, in cncoding the transcripts into the language of theory.
Roughly, wc can describc the cncoding process as follows:

## Input
→ Encoding → Output The input, given explicitly, corresponds to one or more units of the transcript.
'Thesc units can be individual words, scqucnces of words separated by pauses, phrases, sentences, or cven complete protocols.
The output must belong to an a priori, explicitly given, set of alternative cncodings.

In the idcal case, the encoding would be done by a computer program, for thcn wc would know cxactly what knowledgc and procedures were being used, and with what theoretical entailments.
In the case of the human coder, too, it would be highly desirable to be able to specify what inferences and knowledge are used to reach the encoding decisions.

'The theoretic and practical problems of using natural language definitions in sciencc is discussed in depth by Mandler and Kessen (1959). Λs wc have alrcady shown carlier in this chapter, it is possible (and, of course, desirable) to base the cncoding categorics on a fornmal task-analysis in terms of a spacc of knowledge states and a set of operators.
Among their many advantages, such cxplicit and formal definitions of encoding categories will hclp incrcase coding reliability.

## Context-Frec
Encoding 'The cntanglement of data with theory is reduccd and simplificd to the extent that cach output is independent of thosc that prccedc and follow it.
In order to secure complete independence the cncoding operations for cach output would have to be distinct, and would not refcr to the same recordcd observations.
When the encoding is done by humans, such independence is almost impossible to attain, for coders may recall information from previous inputs to bias their encodings of subscquent inputs.
We have already adverted to this problem above and will discuss it in more detail later in this chapter.
'These rather general and abstract remarks can uscfully be illustrated by a few cxamples.
Memory-span Task.
In the mcmory-span task, subjccts are instructed to repeat back a series of verbal symbols (e.g., digits) in exactly the order in which they were presented.
If a complete match is attained, the output is "correct," else "incorrect." 'The encoding operation is the result of a sequential match betwcen the input string and the recorded verbalized response string.
Free Recall of Lists.
Free recall of lists (e.g., lists of words) requires a slightly more complex encoding operation.
'The recorded verbalizations may be of three kinds: (1) words on the stimulus list; (2) incorrect 'guesses" of words thought to be on the list; and (3) other verbalizations, like, "lct me scc," "I am pretty sure there was an animal name on the list," or the like.
Nobody seriously qucstions that distinctions among these three kinds of verbalizations can be encoded reliably and veridically by people.
Yet a computer program capable of discriminating between the second and third categories would be distinctly non-trivial.
Story Recall.
Encoding of verbalizations becomes still more complex if the task is to recall texts or stories.
The meaning of a text is not captured uniqucly in a specific string of words, but can bc expressed, at lcast approximately, in a large number of different ways.
For purposes of encoding, it is necessary to have a theoretical framework within which the semantics of the text can be characterized.
Suppose that the mcaning of the text is represented by propositions (Kintsch, 1974).
Prior to encoding, the stimulus text is analyzed into a set of propositions that convey its mcaning.
'Then, during cncoding, the verbalizations of the subject are converted into propositions, and these are compared for semantic cquivalence with the propositions previously derived from the text by the experimenter.
In most applications of this coding method, the number of propositions successfully identified as matching tcxt mcanings is counted, and propositions that cannot be matched arc not evaluated.

## Other
Issues From our discussion to this point, we can identify a number of issues that should bc discusscd in more depth.

## Selection
of Information for Coding 'Therc are many characteristics that are desired in a transcript.
The transcript should be usable by investigators with different theories and rescarch foci.
Hence, transcription should not rely on theoretical assumptions that are controversial or not generally shared by the relevant investigators.
All inforimation that is important to subscquent cncoding into thc language of different theories should be preserved in the transcript.
Our discussion here is limited to situations where a single person is performing a task, and does not include those where two or more persons arc working togcthcr, as in reaching a decision (Paync, 1976).
Wc also ignore the influence of the experimenter on the subject.

(Sce Ochs (1979) for a discussion of parent-child interactions.) Even though most cognitive tasks clicit relatively simple bchavior and occur in rather static pcrceptual environments, not all of the relevant information can be retained if the transcription task is to be manageable.
Through an analysis of the task itself, the information about behavior and cnvironment that is relevant to task performancc can usually be defined fairly well.
Information about the physical environment, especially if the stimulus is partly or wholly visual, is important and sometimcs difficult to capture adequately.
It is important because it is part of the definition of the stimulus. lt is difficult to capture because such visual stimuli arc often not casy to describe verbally, and because the subject's referenccs to these stimuli are often not casy to disambiguate without a rather complete record of the information that is perccptually available.
Cognitive tasks vary widely in the amount of task-rclcvant information that is available perccptually and in the stability or change of this information while the task is being performed.
Many tasks (chess, 'Tower of Hanoi) employ boards or other physical devices that are altered by the subject's moves.

For those problems that use a static display of information it is not necessary to record changes in the cnvironment in the transcription of bchavior.
Purely mental problems, like mental multiplication with oral presentation of the problem, force the subject to keep the necessary information in memory.
Similarly, for retrospective reports, since the original stimulus will no longer be available, the problem as presented should usually provide a sufficient context for interpreting the transcriptions.
The verbalizations of adults can gencrally be transcribed into ordinary words.
Dictionary words may not adcquately describe the verbalizations of young children (Ochs, 1979).
However, cven in adult specch several aspccts of the recorded verbalizations, such as intonation patterns and pauses, are not casily transcribed.
Furthermore, encoding the stress and duration of cach word and pause is tremendously timeconsuming and costly.
Hence, it is important to make a thcoretically sound and uncontroversial abstraction from the raw protocol that allows reliable coding and captures the relevant information for subscquent coding operations. Λ rather similar problem is encountered in describing eye movements.
The dircction of the gaze can be recorded continuously, so that it becomes important to find a timc interval over which to integratc, in order to make the data manageable.
Becausc, for static displays, the eyes move by sudden discrete saccades, thc sequence of directions of gaze betwccn saccades and the duration of cach of the intervals can be taken as the basic mcasurcments (Winikoff, 1967).

## "Contamination"
of Data by 'Theory Beauty may lie in the eyc of thc bcholdcr, but it is a major goal of scicntific mcthod that truth should lie in the data — should be objcctive rather than subjective.
As applied to verbal data, what does this requirement of objectivity mcan?
It cannot mcan that data are collected and encoded without regard to cxisting theory.
We have already scen why that cannot and should not be done. Λ single verbal protocol is not an island to itself, but a link in a whole chain of evidencc, strctching far into the past and the future, that gradually develops, molds, and modifies our scientific theories.
It needs to be processed with full attention to these linkages.
The proccss must be vicwed as a repcated cycle (or helix, if we believe there is constant progress along the axis). Λt any given time certain concepts and propositions are given credence as providing more or less plausible accounts of a body of phenomena.
These concepts and propositions may constitute a single theory, or a collection of competing theories, or cven a hierarchy of theories, from very general (but weak) to very spccific (but strong), and from highly probable to barely plausible.
In the liıniting, but not infrequent, casc, data may cxist that exhibit clear regularities without any current theory to describe or explain theimn.
Such regularities often lead to the induction of new theories (Simon, Langley, & Bradshaw, 1981).
The existing theories suggest new observations and experiments to be made, cither with the aim of choosing between alternative hypotheses, or of strengthening (or weakening) the credibility of a specific theory when there are no competitors, or of improving and cxtending an existing theory.
If existing thcorics cxplain only part of the phenomnena, with a good deal of residual "error variance" or "noise," as is almost always the case, then the new observations may introduce new variables and mcasurcments, soinctimes depcnding on ncw instrumentation, in an effort to account for the unexplained variance.
Power and Parsimony.
'T'he "quality" of a particular thcory in the facc of a body of cvidence must be judged by the rclation betwcen the amount of variancc the thcory cxplains and the number of degrees of frecdom (parameters) requircd to fit thc data.
Exactly what figurc of mcrit, what function of variancc cxplained and dcgrees of freedom cmployed, should be used to evaluate thcories is a deep problem in the modern theory of statistics, and there is at present no consensus on the precise answer.
But cveryonc docs agrce that "power" and "parsimony" are the important characteristics of a successful theory, and that there is some tradeoff between these two measures.
If the power of a theory is enhanccd by adding ncw variables or paramctcrs, its parsimony is decrcased; if it is simplified to incrcase parsımony, power will usually be lost.
The best we can aspire to, in scientific inquiry, are large increases in power in exchange for very small losses in parsimony.
On rare occasions, new formulations are found in some domain that greatly incrcase power without loss of parsimony.
'l’hese are the true "scientific revolutions" of which so much has been written in recent ycars.
In the literature of statistics, most attention has been paid to the situation where two theorics are competing to explain the same body of data.
If the two theories are cqually parsimonious, have the same numbers of degrees of frecdoın, then obviously the most powerful is to be preferred.
If one is more parsimonious than the other, then some tradcoff ratio can be used to make the choicc.
'The more complex, and we belicve, the more common case is one in which only one theory has been put forth, and the task is to cvaluate it in the light of new cvidence.
To scc how this might be done, we must make an cxcursion into Bayes' 'Theorem. Λ Bayesian Framework.
Evcn though wc scldom havc available adequate data to apply it numerically, Bayes' 'T’heorem provides us with a framcwork within which wc can cxamine morc closcly thc issues of power and parsimony.
We will not try to attach a spurious quantification to our argument, but simply use Bayes' Theorem as a qualitative guide.
'The credence we place in a hypothesis, say $\mathrm { H } _ { \mathrm { i } } ,$ on the basis of all of our previous knowledge and cvidence is called, in Baycsian thcory, its $a$ priori probability, which we will denote by ${ \sf P } _ { 0 } ^ { } ( { \sf H } _ { \mathrm { i } } )$ Whcn we analyze ncw data and throw it into the balance, revising this initial probability for cach of the hypotheses we arc cntcrtaining, wc calculatc a ncw probability, thc posterior probability, for cach hypothesis.
Wc will call this $\mathrm { P _ { \mathrm { 1 } } ( H _ { \mathrm { i } } ) }$ Bayes''Thcorem providcs a rule for calculating these latter probabilities.
To make this calculation, we must also know the probability that cach hypothesis would produce the data actually obscrved.
'This probability, callcd the productive probability of the hypothesis for the data, will be denoted by $\mathrm { P _ { n } ( D ; H _ { i } ) }$ Consider two urns (hypotheses) containing four balls cach.

Matters arc arranged so that it is cqually likcly that we will draw a ball from cither urn.
