Sincc, in this simple casc, the probability of drawing cach of the balls is exactly the same, and since therc are thrce white balls in the first urn and only onc in the sccond, the answer is obviously 3/4.
More gencrally, and for less simple cases, Bayes' 'Theoreın gives the posterior probability that the ball came from the first urn $( \mathsf { H } _ { 1 } ^ { } )$ was correct) as: $$ \begin{array} { r l } { \mathrm { P } _ { 1 } ^ { \mathrm { \phantom { } } } ( \mathrm { H } _ { 1 } ^ { \phantom { } } ; \mathrm { W } ) { = } [ \mathrm { P } _ { \mathrm { \ p } } ^ { \mathrm { \phantom { } } } ( \mathrm { W } ; \mathrm { H } _ { 1 } ^ { \phantom { } } ) \mathrm { P } _ { 0 } ^ { \phantom { } } ( \mathrm { H } _ { 1 } ^ { \phantom { } } ) ] / } & { { } } \\ { \mathrm { [ P } _ { \mathrm { \ p } } ^ { \mathrm { \phantom { } } } ( \mathrm { W } ; \mathrm { H } _ { 1 } ^ { \phantom { } } ) \mathrm { P } _ { 0 } ^ { \mathrm { \phantom { } } } ( \mathrm { H } _ { 1 } ^ { \phantom { } } ) { + } \mathrm { P } _ { \mathrm { \ p } } ^ { \mathrm { \phantom { } } } ( \mathrm { W } ; \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } ^ { \phantom { } } ) \mathrm { P } _ { 0 } ^ { \phantom { } } ( \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } ^ { \phantom { } } ) ] } & { { } } \\ { { = } [ 3 / 4 \mathrm { \ x } \mathrm { ~ } 1 / 2 ] / \left[ 3 / 4 \mathrm { \ x } \mathrm { ~ } 1 / 2 + \right]} \mathrm { 1 } / 4 \mathrm { \ x } \mathrm { ~ } 1 / 2 = & { { } 3 / 4 } \end{array} $$ Of course the formula can bc generalizcd to an arbitrary sct of hypotheses.
'Then the denominator simply becomnes the sum, over all of the hypotheses, of the products of their productive probabilities for the observed data by their prior probabilities.
When we arc dealt a hand of thirtcen spades in bridge, we have to choose betwcen the hypothesis that the deck has been well shuffled, and the hypothesis that the dealer has played a trick on us.
The productive probability of the first hypothesis (the hypothesis that a well-shuffled deck will produce a deal of thirteen spades to one player) is very low, but the prior probability—since we have known our friend, the dealer, as an honcst person — is quite high.
On the other hand, the productive probability of the sccond hypothesis (that a trickster will deal out a hand all of onc suit) is quite high, although its prior probability is low.
Bayes' Theorem tells us what credence to put in our friend's honesty after the deal, on the basis of these probabilities.
'The productive probabilities can be computed from the thcory of combinations, but the prior probabilities must be based on our previous experience with human nature in general and our friend in particular.
Implications of Bayes' Theorem for Coding.
What does Bayes' Theorem have to tell us about the problems of recording, cncoding, and interpreting verbal data?
First, it has something important to say about the venerable problem of prcdiction versus postdiction.
What difference does it make whcther we announce a hypothcsis first, then gather and analyzc data to tcst it, or whcthcr wc gather thc data and inducc the hypothesis from it?
T’he received wisdom is that the hypothesis is to be given grcater credcncc in the first case than in the second.
But is this correct?
We can apply Bayes' Theorcm thus.
Before we gathered the new data, the hypothesis in question (whether enunciated or not) had a certain prior probability.
The hypothesis also has a definite productive probability for the new data.
'The same may be said for any other hypotheses that had been or could have been gencrated.
Hence we can calculate the posterior probability of our hypothesis in the usual way, and the time when it was generated simply does not enter into the calculation (Simon, 1977).
But the common wisdom on this mattcr is not wholly indefensible.
Assume that hypotheses are constructed by some process, which we will refer to as the generator.
The gencrator will produce hypotheses on the basis of the information available to it, and presumably will be so designed as to produce hypotheses with high prior probabilities (in the light of this information) before it produces hypotheses with low probabilities.
If the generator has produced a particular hypothesis before certain new data were available, then it is rcasonable to suppose that the prior probability of that hypothesis was substantial.
If, however, the gencrator is given the new data as well, and allowed to run until it produces a hypothesis compatible with thesc data, it may put forward candidates that would have been assigned low priors before the new data were gathered.
Hencc, we cannot really assume equal prior probabilities in the two cases.
This is presumably the basis for our greater confidence in a hypothesis that has made successful predictions, than in one that has been constructed with the data it has to fit already in vicw.
'The former gencrally comes to the new data with a higher prior probability than the latter.
This does not in any way imply, however, that data gathered prior to the formnulation of a hypothesis has no probative value for the hypothesis.
Even though we had not considered the possibility that our friend was a trickster bcfore wc picked up our hand of thirteen spades, and only formulated the hypothesis at that moment, the fact that we were dealt that hand markedly incrcases the probability of the hypothesis from its previous level, and its posterior may now be quite large as a result of this evidencc, and cven in the face of a vcry low prior.
The common vicw that hypotheses must bc formulated before cxpcriments are run in order for the data to have value as cvidcnce is simply false.
However, how much credence we should place in them on the basis of the cvidence may depend on whether or not they were thought of first.
In the use of protocol data, it is a common practicc, and often a necessary onc, to cxtract the coding categorics and proccdures from a study of the protocol itself.
'T’he model of the process that we wish to test may be constructed aftcr cxamination of thc same data.
T'hese proccdures obviously consume some of the degrces of frecdom of the

## 284
Protocol Analysis data, but if the coding categories and proccdures are relatively simple and highly objective, and if thc model to be tested is parsimonious in relation to the volume of data to be cxplained, then there is nothing circular about proceding in this way. Λ good fit of model to data still contributes to the posterior probability of the model, and the more parsimnonious the model and proccdures, and the more voluminous the data, the grcater the increment in the credibility of the model.
In the same way, it is often necessary, when coding protocol segments, to take into account a wider or narrower context of cach segment.
Again, this practice reduces the degrees of freedom in the data, but does not, in any absolute sense, compromise the coding procedure as a way of testing models of the data.
Necessity should not be made a virtuc.
Data cannot be uscd twice as evidence in Bayes' formula—first in calculating the prior probability, and again in calculating the productive probability of the hypothesis being tested.
Hencc, when degrees of freedom in the data are absorbed by their usc prior to testing, their absorption should be taken into account in the testing process.
In general, formal statistical methods for doing this are not available, but conceptually, the case is clear.
Moreover, a given body of data will provide stronger evidence for or against a model if the coding categories and procedures have already been constructed from analysis of the task domain, or from previously gathered protocols of other subjects, and if the model has also been formulated on the basıs of other evidence.
Lct us now return to the situation, introduced in the previous section, where we are not choosing betwecn alternative hypotheses, but have at most one theory to fit our data.
Without alternative hypotheses, we can not apply Bayes' formula; but we can imagine a surrogate hypothesis, with very low prior and productive probabilitics for the data, to reprcsent all of thesc unknown alternatives.
Suppose that the hypothcsis wc are considcring (whether invented bcfore or after wc saw the data) cxplains the data very successfully and parsimoniously.
Then its productive probability for thc data will be high.
Examining Baycs' formula, we sce that since the remaining terms in the denominator will be close to zero, numcrator and denominator will be nearly cqual, with thc conscqucnce that the posterior probability of our hypothesis will be close to unity.
Wc do not wish to push this conclusion too far.
But it does illustrate how data can provide credibility to a single hypothesis, cven in the absence of explicit alternatives with which to compare it.
Morcover, the argument again does not depend on whether the hypothesis was gencrated before or after the data were produced.
Disconfirmation of Theories.
Contrary to the doctrine of the Popperians, there is no "sudden death" of thcories.
Since observations have to bc encoded and interpreted, using existing theorctical knowledge for that purpose, before they can confront thcorics, the failure of a theory to fit observations precisely does not mean that it has to be rcjected outright.
Perhaps the fault docs not lic in thc theory, but in some of the auxiliary, mcthodological, and theorctical assumptions that have been made in thc fitting process.
Classical Newtonian mechanics was not rejected simply bccause soımne plancts deviated from the cxpected Newtonian paths.
Instcad, the implicit assumption in the calculations, that there were no unobserved planets, was tentatively rejected, and a search undertaken for bodies that might account for the deviations.
'Twice the theory was saved in this way (by thc discoveries of Neptunc and Uranus); on the third occasion (cxplanation of the preccssion of the perihclion of Mercury), it gave way to a compcting thcory, Gencral Rclativity, that cxplained the phcnomcnon without postulating a new planet.
The case of the overthrow of a theory by a completely new one is dramatic, but comparatively rare.
More often, unexplaincd variancc is dcalt with by secking ncw variables (as in the Newtonian casc) to account for it.
Hencc the argument for a thcory, that it explains a good deal of variance parsimoniously, is usually more important than the argument against it, that it lcaves much variance uncxplaincd—unless, of coursc, there is a competing theory that does a better job.
'The practice of science cxcmplifies the practical wisdom of politics that "you can't beat somcthing with nothing." General Lessons for Methodology.
'The parsimony of a theory is as hard to cvaluate as its power.
Degrces of frecdom are used up not only in estimating the parameters of the model from empirical data, but also in the process of encoding and interprcting the data.
Even in a simple physical casc, the mcasurcmcnt of tempcraturc, say, a grcat many degrees of frcedom lurk in the proccdures for calibrating thc thermomcters and recording the temperature in the expcrimental situation.
Since the contemporary experimcntalist docs his work against an cnormous background of hcat mcasurcment and instrument calibration by his predecessors, hc is provided with a standardizcd cnvironment, and does not "consume" degrces of freedom in fashioning his own instruments.
The case is quite different in analyzing protocols for a new cognitive task, one that has not bcen studicd cxtensively in the laboratory.
Large numbers of degrees of freedom may be uscd up in the carly steps of data recording and data encoding, with the result that the final interpretation of the data and its matching against the theory may appear to reflect mainly hindsight — pulling out of the data the hypotheses that have been implicitly hidden in it by the data interpretation process.
This is the core of validity in the criticisms sometimes levcled against computer simulation of thinking, although it hardly justifies the cxtravagant and usually false claim that "1f you are given a verbal protocol, you can always write a computer program that will simulate it." How can the problem of parsimony be solved?
The answer for verbal protocols seems to be exactly the same as the answer for any other kind of data.
It has several components.
1.
In choosing data for transcription, and in transcribing and encoding them, the theoretical commitments that are made should be kept as small and weak as possible.
We have alrcady cmphasized this principle throughout our discussion.
2.
'The theoretical assumptions and presuppositions underlying the data analysis should bc made explicit.
'This is casy when the analysis is done automatically; difficult when it is done by humans.
3.
'The data analysis process should bc not only objcctive and reproducible, but it should remain constant from one protocol to another.
In this way, the degrees of freedoın that are used by these procedures arc absorbed by a constantly growing body of data.
This can be done by dividing the protocol material into two parts, developing thc data anlysis scheme on one half, and tcsting it against the other half.
4.
Convergent proccdures should be used wherever possible.
For example, as much as possible of the cncoding language and concepts should be derived from an analysis of the task cnvironment, independent of the problem spaces defined by the subjects.
5.
Constant and invariant data analysis proccdures should be used over large bodies of data.
It is much casicr to build a consistent ad hoc theory to cxplain a protocol of 1l scgmcnts than one of 200 segments.
6.
Even where different thcories arc needed to cxplain bchavior in different tasks, the theories should share as many common clements and conponents as possiblc, so that a (wcaker) gcncral theory can be abstracted from the specific ones.
7.
Even where different theories arc needed to cxplain the behavior of different subjects in a given task, the theories should also share as many common clements and components as possible, so that a theory of the "representative subject" (the American college sophomore?) can be constructed.
Examples as Evidence.
Protocol analysis sometimes consists largely of extracting cxamples of concepts or processes from the verbalization as evidence for theories that predict them. Λs Bayes' 'Theorem shows us, the contribution of such examples to the credibility of a theory depends on what alternative explanations are available.
'The recent mcthodological disputc about language acquisition in apes is an interesting case in point.
Much of the important evidence for apes' ability to combine signs crcatively into novel constructs comes from anccdotes (Scidenberg & Petitto, 1979).
For example, the chimpanzce Washoc combined the signs for "water" and "bird" to refer to a duck, and the gorilla Koko combined the signs for "cookie" and "rock" for a stale cookie.
Out of context, these episodes seem to yield rather strong cvidence for the creative use of language by apes.
However, Seidenberg and Petitto (1979, p.
182) point out that the water bird example is less persuasive if the ape also combined water and bird with other signs (c.g., water shoe, water banana, cookie bird, ctc.).
A chimpanzee named Nim (Terrace ct al., 1978) combined signs into many such permutations. Λlthough the combinations are not all idiomatic, there is no way to tell whether they were mcaningful to the animal; thcy may have been random.

## RELIABILITY
AND VALIDITY OF ENCODING A ccntral task in using verbally rcportcd information is to makc thc encoding process as objective as possible.
Without appropriate safeguards, the encoder, exposed to a scrics of ambiguous verbal statements, may encodc them with a bias toward his own preferred interpretation.
Context providcs a principal source of disambiguation of verbal information.

## a dark
ball Without context, a codcr might have grcat difficulty in deciding what objects should be regardcd as instances of the concept defined by this phrase.

As a sccond example, in a problem-solving experiment, a subject says:

In both situations the encoder knows that he is encoding verbalizations taken from a think-aloud protocol from a concept attainment cxperiment.
In the first situation, the cncoder is asked if a verbalization is a statement of the correct hypothesis (c.g., "blue and round").

Now the encoding can proceed in a quite definite way from the information in the protocol. Λ computer program called HEARSΛY (Rcddy & Newell, 1974), developed for automatic recognition of continuous human spccch, provides a useful metaphor for thinking about the encoding problem.
The spcech HEARSΛY recognized consisted of instructions to make moves in a chess gamc.

## Encoding
Process and Encoders Encoding is often cvaluated by tcsts of reliability—agreement between different persons cncoding independently of each other.
But reliability is not enough.
In this section we will discuss some problcims and issues that arisc cven when high inter-coder agrecment is achieved.
We will be conccrned with biases toward the confirmation of hypotheses that have been put forward, inferences of what the subject must have said, rather than what he did say, and problems of restricting the influence of previous encoded information on subscquent coding decisions.
Independence of Fncoding Judgments. Λftcr a protocol is divided into separate scgments, one or more encodings must be generated for cach segment.
Wc arc interested in ways for climinating or greatly reducing the dependence among encodings of different segments so as not to lose degrees of freedom in the data.
The problem arises because human coders remember their previous encodings, and other information about carlier segments.
Traditionally, coding judgments are made about scgments in the order they were verbalized.
It is not uncommon for a subject to verbalizc an intention, like "I want to gct the first row in order," or a concept like, "I think it must be small red squares," and then make later reference to it, like, "I still think it is that," or "I am thinking about the same hypothesis." It would be incorrect to regard these subscquent verbalizations as wholly independent cvidence that the subject was heeding the hypothesis of 'srnall, red squares." The later verbalization is cvidence that he is heeding the same hypothesis as before, but doesn't provide new evidence of what that hypothesis was.
Not all instances of such cross reference are as explicit as this one, but they all pose essentially the same problem.
A possible solution to this probleı involves two things.
During the segmentation, units should be defined that are large enough that all information for making an encoding dccision is contained in a single segment.
For certain encoding decisions, like assessing strategies, this may mean that the entire protocol is a unit.
Later, we will propose an alternative approach of establishing encoding categories that can be assessed from smaller segments.
Sccond, segments should be encoded in random order, thus climinating the possibility that the encoder will rely on information in preceding scgments to make subsequent decisions. Λ computer-based support system for making such encodings is described in the next section.
Bias and Inference.
'lwo types of bias are of particular interest and concern.
'The first results from the encoders having prior knowledge of the hypotheses being tested.
'The sccond results from the encoders assuming that subjccts will think in the same ways that they do.
With respcct to the first, thc best situation is onc in which the coders are naive with respcct to thc cxpcrimental design and the hypotheses.
Of course this is unimportant when the protocol information is very cxplicit and clcar, as it is in many problem-solving protocols.
But for ambiguous and brief protocol segments, the danger of bias may be scrious, and inter-coder agreement does not mcasure coding validity.
In some recent studies (cf.
Wacrn, 1979) cxplicit steps were taken to keep the coders fromn knowing the design or the hypotheses.
'l’he second type of bias arises because encoding often requires at least simple inferences, and assumes that the subjects made the same infercnces.
In general, this is a quite valid assumption, uscful and cven neccssary for understanding other people's thought processes.
Again, it becomes problematic when thc coder is faced with an ambiguous or schematic statement.

Several coders with similar backgrounds, yet different from the background of the subject, could give the same incorrect interpretations.
Even if the inference is "correct," it is not determined by the recorded verbalization.
In the next section we will discuss some methods for restricting the inferential activity of the encoder.

## Encoding
Reliability We turn now to methods for cnsuring that the mapping of input to coding categories is reliable and does not vary among encoders.
In statistical terms, we wish to show that inter-coder agrecment is bcttcr than chance, and also that the differenccs betwcen cncoders are not systematic.

Encoding Segments or Phrases.
Many of the difficultics encountered in carfier coding methods can be climinated by coding individual segments of protocols.

We should not gencrally be satisfied, however, with a single aggregate mcasure of coding reliability.
Such a measure will mainly reflect thc very frequcnt coding categories, and thc encodings of infrequent catcgorics may bc much less—or morc — reliable than the average.

and Semi-Automatic Protocol Analysis It would be highly desirable to automate, wholly or partially, the cncoding of protocols.
In this section, we describe two rescarch cfforts, mentioncd carlicr, that were aimcd at developing such cncoding programs: the PΛS-I and PAS-Il research of Waterman and Newell, and the work on SΛPΛ by Bhaskar and Simon.
We will focus on PΛS-l for several reasons.

Since the SΛPΛ prograin was designcd to be uscd interactively by a human coder, it did not have to address all of these problems.
Fach program was tested on only a single task — SΛPΛ on problems in thermodynamics and PΛS-I on cryptarithmctic problcms.
However, thc principles of design underlying the systemns have broad applicability.
PΛS-I.
The PΛS-l program was designed to produce Problem Behavior Graphs dircctly from segmented protocols.
'T’he program was so structured that information peculiar to thc given task could be separated from gencral information.
In a subscquent version, PΛS-II, rules spccial to a given application could be read into the program.
However, we will mainly describc P∧S-I, which was programmcd to analyzc cryptarithmetic protocols.
The final product of PΛS-I is the Problem Bchavior Graph (PBG), which incorporates scveral theorctical assumptions that constrain its gencration.
However, since PAS-I procccds with its analysis in stages, we can look at the intermediate products also, and see where the theorctical assumptions affect the coding process.
Before PAS-l goes to work on a protocol, a problem space is defined manually, by examination of the task and the protocol.
This problem space delimits the kinds of encodings that can bc derived from the protocol statements.
'Ihe protocol is also scgmented by hand in preparation for the automatic encoding.
'The encoding aimed at by the PΛS systcms was essentially that which Newell and Simon (1972) had previously specified in their manual encodings of protocols—that is, it was to produce a PBG showing the successive states of knowledge attained by the subject and the productions that were executed in proceeding from cach state to the next.
We will first describe the basic sequence of processing in PAS-I.
Next, we will describe some important components in detail.
Finally, we will raise some methodological issues and discuss the results of actual runs with PΛS-1 and the sources of its errors.
Basic Structure.
PAS-I is organized in three separate programs, the latter two operating on the outputs of their predecessors.
'T’he segments of the protocol are first analyzed by the linguistic processor, which encodes the segments into propositions.
The output from the linguistic processor is thc input to the semantic processor, which rccodes the propositions into smaller sets of primitives, and groups the propositional information as inputs and outputs of possible information processes.
Finally, the output of the semantic proccssor is the input of the problem behavior graph generator, which gencrates a PBG for thc protocol.
Each protocol segment is cncoded by the linguistic processor independently of the others (cf. the local cncoding by MPΛS).
Moreover, all further processing is done froın the output of this encoding, without reference to the raw protocol.
Let us consider how a propositional encoding ("semantic elements" in the terminology of Waterman & Newell) can be generated from protocol segments.
Watcrman and Newell usc a keyword grammar to map the protocol segments on propositional clemcnts.
This grammar can be scen as a formal spccification of the sct of linguistic patterns that should be mapped on a given propositional relation.
For cxample, in the cryptarithmctic task, thc subject is sccking to assign a given letter (say, D) to its proper number. Λ protocol segment of the form "D cquals $2 "$ or "Change D to 2" $2 "$ is judged propositionally cquivalent to $" 1 ) \ = \ 2 "$ or "(Eq D) 2)," and is so encoded.
All protocol segments that should be mapped onto "(Eq <letter> <digit>)" are specificd formally by the linguistic proccssor.
Watcrman and Newell (1971) provide the following cxample: <icuer> dircctly followed by <prep1> and then <digit> Start segment with "Change" directly followed by <letter> and the <digit> or <letter> dircctly followed by "cquals" and the <digit>. where <letter> denotes onc of the letters relevant to the task, and where <prepl> refers to a preposition.
"Change" is a kcyword that has to appear literally in the text.
This template would recognize and encode the following segments: D for the 2 Use 1) as the number 2 Change R to 2 Fach i is 5 Fach D equals 5 In the following figure, taken from Waterman and Newell (1971), we can sce how the last sentence above is mapped, as well as some more complete structures.
This type of template grammar thus provides a flexible link between the propositional elements identificd in the task analysis and a large number of different possible protocol segments.
Waterman and Ncwcll (1972) arguc against a full-flcdged linguistic and semantic analysis of protocol segments, for scveral rcasons.
'The most obvious is that such an analysis would be difficult and call for a much more complex program than PΛS-l.
Furthermore, since protocol scgments are often incomplete sentences and not fully grammatical, syntactic information would havc limited use.
They arguc that the PΛS program should be more interactive, expectations bcing gencrated by the carlier parts of the analysis, and used to guide the linguistic analysis on the basis of assumptions of reasonable continuation.
However, the current program analyses cach scgment locally and independently of previous ones— incidentally providing us with uscful information about the feasibility of local encoding.
Evaluation of PAS-I.

SAPA.
In their analysis of problem solving in thermodynamics, Bhaskar and Simon (1977) proposed a semni-automatic system for protocol analysis realized as a computer program (SΛPΛ).
'T’he program incorporates a prediction (predicted problem space and strategy) of the problem solving process in this task domain.
Both the scqucnce in which information will be addressed, and the dccisions that will be reached are predicted.
Figure 6-8 shows the main components of the problem solving proccss incorporatcd in SΛPΛ and the ordcr in which they are predicted to occur.
Figure 6-8 Flow diagram of SAPA program SΛPΛ embodies a rough preliminary model of the subject's problem solving strategy. Λs cach new scgment is taken up, it prompts the coder by predicting the operation the subject will apply next.
If the prediction is correct (the operation expressed or implied by the segment corresponds to that prcdicted by SΛPΛ), thc human coder merely provides, from the protocol, the operator's arguments.
If the prediction is incorrect, the human coder exccutes a "break" in the SAPΛ strategy, which puts the program back on the right track again and then inserts a paraphrase of the uncoded segimnent as a "comment." For the protocol shown below (Tables 6-2 and 6-3), SΛPA does a very good job of anticipating its contents and the order in which they will appear.
The SΛPΛ scheme for these thermodynamics problems rests on the task-dependent assumption (empirically valid for these subjccts) that the solution process will be built around the cquation of conservation of energy, and the special form this cquation takes in cach particular problem.
'The "logic" of the solution process consists in trying to solve successively for the remaining unknowns in this cquation, after it has been specialized to fit the particular conditions of the problem.

## EFFECTIVE
PROTOCOL ANALYSIS PROCEDURES In this concluding scction, we will sum up our discussion by making suggestions as to which approaches to protocol analysis appear to have the highest potential of success.
Wc have identified a number of problems, and suggested solutions for some of them: We will now try to show how these solutions follow from (or are at least consist with) our theoretical model of the processes of verbalization.

## Matching
Coding Categories to Verbalizations Our model asserts that verbalization is a reflection of the heeded information.
If that is so, then the more directly an cncoding scheme can capturc the units and structurc of thc verbalizations, the better-for several reasons.
First, the closcr the match betwcen cncoding categories and verbalizations, thc casier it will be to encode them, and the more rcliable will bc thc cncoding. Λutomating thc cncoding will also be casicr.
Second, thc closer the match, the less will be the necd to use non-local context to make encoding decisions.
Third, the closer the match, the largcr will be the fraction of the information in the verbalization that can be cncodcd. ln the idcal case, onc should bc able to regcncrate the actual verbalizations from the information contained in the cncoding, using a simple gramımar.
We have argued carlier that local cncoding will usually be adequate.
Howcver, new data may show that somc internal states can only be assesscd by using a much larger context than we have becn considering.
Wc see two substantial objcctions to the approach we have been describing and advocating, and a third objection that we consider wholly invalid.
Let us start with the latter.
It is still the case that protocols are often collected and analysed in the absence of a cognitive model defining what verbalizations would constitute cvidence for cach coding category.
We believe that this procedure wilì be used less and less as the need for a theoretical base for encoding is understood.
Of the other two objcctions against our approach, the most serious is that it is cxcccdingly time-consuming.
Especially when only selected aspccts of the cognitive process are of interest, it may require inordinate effort to analyze all protocol scgments in detail.
We will show later how selected aspccts can be cxtracted from a protocol at the segment level without requiring a full-blown analysis of the entire protocol.
Another objcction is that we may want to abstract or extract gencralizable entitics, like reprcsentations, rules, strategics, and so on, instcad of encoding segment by scgment.
Evidence about such entities may be scattered through the protocol, so that their assessment requires simultaneous consideration of the entire cognitive processing activity.
It may bc methodologically admissible to make such global assessments, but we would argue against it on theoretical grounds.
We will argue that the protocol contains more reliable basic information that can be used as data for the assessment at the more general level.
In Chapter 7, we will provide several cxaımnples to show how goals, intermcdiate results and gencrated problein-configurations can be encoded separately and how an analysis of a large number of such encodings can support a general representation.
Wc will also discuss briefly the use of expcrimental mcthods to increase the probability that all subjects will hccd a widc rangc of stimulus instanccs.
When subjccts all attend to the same information, their responses allow us to cvaluate the generalizability of the proposed representations and strategies.

## Verbalization
of General Knowledge and Rules Generalized entities, like representations and procedures, are dircctly verbalized only under cxtraordinary circumstances. Λ subject will not usually say, "I will consider all logically possible combinations of variables X and Y that have feature Z." More often, subjects explore specific instances that wc can describe as being combinations of X and Y with feature Z.It is also only rarely that subjects statc cxplicity that a new knowledge structure thcy havc generated is an instancc of a general process or procedure with such and such characteristics.
Protocols provide many instances of knowledge structures, but the generality and scope of the processes that generated them must be inferred, and is seldom indicated explicitly in the protocols.
It is quite possible, of course, for subjects to use abstract concepts, relations, knowledge, and rules that are gencral and gencralizable in the sense that they apply to many situations and contexts. Λn obvious cxample is the verbalization of an hypothesis in a concept learning experiment.
Verbalized knowledge clements are also general.
In cryptarithmetic, Subject S3 of Newell and Simon verbalized the following relation: $$ \mathrm { " S i n c e ~ l ) + \ l > = G , G \ m u s t \ b e \ e v e n . ^ { \cdot } } $$ an inference that applies in several situations in this and other cryptarithmetic problems.
An indirect verbalization of a rule can be identificd in the following verbal report on mental multiplication, "First I will put the largest number on top," and the verbalization of a goal, "Have largest number on top." It is often casy and tempting to encode information logically.
However, it is psychologically possible and cven plausible that a concept like "largest" will not be generated or heeded unless the number cxcceds some limit of magnitude.
'I’he preconditions of this rule will not be met by numbers differing by only a small amount, contradicting the logical interpretation.
Hence, abstract or general statements cannot be translated into a formal representation without careful consideration of the context.
'T’hus, in the context that this rule and goal was gencrated and verbalized, onc of the numbers was noted as being the largest.
Yet, under what circumstances this verbalization will occur rcquires further spccification.
Knowledge and rules reside in ITM.
In order to be hecded and to influence the cognitive process, they need to be accessed by appropriate retricval cues.
Even though wc have been able to identify them in a protocol on one problem, we cannot be certain that they will be accessed and used on other problems.
Mcta-comments are another source of gencral statcinents about the cognitive processes. Λ description of a general procedure for dealing with a class of problcms is not a mcta-commcnt, for it draws on prcviously stored information.
A clear case of a mcta-comment is a subjcct's attempt to verbalize regularitics in his own cognitive processes.
We argued carlier that these verbalizations are often of limited valuc, and arc clearly abstractions, influenccd by the episodic information that the subject can retrieve at the time.
Thc best singlc test for distinguishing meta-comments from verbalizations of current processes derives from thcir role in subscquent processcs.
A verbalized proccdure, likc a recipc, will be accessed cach time the corresponding cognitive process is executed.
It corresponds to the representation of the relevant knowledge. Λ meta-comment will most likcly not be acccssed and used to direct subscquent bchavior.

## Conclusion
In this chapter wc have shown how the information hecded during a cognitive process can be identified by an analysis of the corresponding verbalizations.
In protocol analysis, we arc trying to infer what information was heeded as input for the observed verbalization.
'Through a carcful task analysis it is possible to definc a priori a space of possible encodings representing the information relevant to the task.
'Ihen, encoding protocols involves finding the catcgory that cxpresses the same information as the verbalization.
In the carlier chapters, cspccially Chapter 5, we argued that 'TΛ verbalizations closcly match the flow of attention to infornation.
By locating language production units and linguistic structures, the sequence of heeded information can be uncovered.
Although the majority of encoding schemes define their categories so that individual protocol segments can bc cncoded, many schemes do not attempt to uncover the heeded information, but seck to infer directly the processes that generated the hecded inforination.
Wc arguc that, whencver possible, the original encoding should reflect as closely as possible the verbalized information, and should preferably be derived by automatic or scmiautomatic mcans.
Once verbalizations are converted to formal cncodings, theoretical proposals for representations, processes and strategies can be introduced to provide parsimonious accounts for the protocol data. # TECHNIQUES OF PROTOCOL ANALYSIS EXAMPLES In the previous chapter we developed a gencral framework for considering thc cncoding and analysis of protocols.
We raised and discussed a number of theoretical issues, and illustrated various forms of protocel analysis.
In this chapter, we will cxaminc a substantial numbcr of concrete examples of protocol analysis to illuminate the more general questions that have bcen raised, and to provide further illustrátions of techniqucs and issues.
We begin with a discussion of informal mcthods of analysis.
Then we discuss methods for inferring théoretical entities from protocols.
Finally we will revicw studies exploring the reliability, validity and gencralizability of protocol data, and discuss future dircction of these kinds of analyscs.

## INFORMAL
PROTOCOL ANALYSIS In order to construct a thcoretical framework and coding scheme for a set of protocols, pilot work will bc ncccssary to develop thc coding categorics.
Even during thesc preliminary and cxploratory phases of analysis there cxist general methods that are useful both for understanding the cognitive processes reflccted in the protocols and for approaching the definition of coding categories.
Verbalizations cannot convcy more information than was available to thc proccss that produced them.
Protocol analysis may involve categorizing the verbalizations according to the processes that could have gencrated them.
We wish to providc some guidelincs for making this classification uniquely and unambiguously.
Wc assume a hicrarchy of processes, thc simplest bcing operations like Copy, which transfer information that is available from the senses or in memory.
At the first step, we encode cach verbalization in terms of the simplest process that could account for it.
A verbalization may be a literal copy of information that is presented or has been ımnemorizcd previously.
In this case, the verbalization may or may not be gencrated without being processed semantically.
It will seldom be possible to infer with certainty whether it was understood or parroted.

## USING
A THEORY FOR PROTOCOL PREDICTION Whcre a theory of the cognitive processes undcr investigation has already becn postulated, sevcral kinds of prcdictions can bc madc about the information that subjects will attend to and rcport orally.
On the one hand, a thcory can yicld wcak predictions of the kinds of information that will be hceded in performing the task, without prcdicting the sequcnce in which information will bc attendcd to.
On the othcr hand, a theory can permit inferences about the sequences of processes required to reach a corrcct solution of the task, and thereby yicld strong predictions that only those sequenccs of processes would appcar in subjects' protocols.
To make these predictions as precise as possible, the theory of task performance necds to bc complemcnted by a thcory of verbalization, so that wc know what part of the information that is hecded has a high probability of bcing verbalizcd, and what part has a low probability.
We have tricd in the carlier chapters of this book to providc such a complementary theory.
'To test a hypothesis of the first, or weaker type, we necd to compare the sct of statcments implied by that hypothesis with the statements implied by competing proccsses.
'T’he union of these sets defines the totality of coding catcgories that needs to be considered in encoding the protocols in a manner that is both comprehensive and neutral among the hypotheses. Λ hypothesis of the sccond, or stronger, type predicts cither a uniquc sequence of verbalizations or a set of acceptable scquences.
Such a sequcncc or sct can also be represented as a transition network, a represcntation that may bc attractive for somc purposes.
'Thc two representations, as sct of sequcnces or nctwork, are of course logically cquivalent.
Altcrnative hypotheses can bc cxplicated in thc same way as sets of sequences of verbalizations, and the actual scquences can readily be compared with those prcdicted by the different hypotheses.
To make thesc considerations concrete, wc will carry through in some detail analyses of two kinds of examples, First, we will show how an analysis of identified instances of gencrated information can allow us to derive and evaluate hypotheses regarding the representation of information.
Ihen wc will show, by mcans of examples, how hypotheses about processes and strategies can be used to predict the order in which information is verbalized.

## CHARACTERISTICS
OF GENERATED INFORMATION: REPRESENTATIONS Determining what representation a subject is using in a problem solving task is often a difficult and subtle matter.

First, we will explore different methods for characterizing heeded information using the Eight Puzzle as our example.
Then we will show how representations of the 'Tower of Hanoi can be inferred from protocols.

## The
Eight Puzzle First, we need to describe the Fight Puzzle and say somcthing about the experiment that produced the protocols (Ericsson, 1975b).
In the Eight Puzzle, subjects are prescnted with a 3x3 matrix of numbered square tiles (Figure 7-la).
By sliding one of the directly adjacent tiles into the empty space, the arrangement of tiles can be changed.
Subjects are instructed to achieve the goal arrangcment (Figure 7-1b).
In this cxperimcnt, subjects were given different starting configurations, but all asked to achieve the particular goal configuration shown in the figurc.
Figure 7-1 Example of a configuration for the Eight Puzzle (left); this is to be transformed into a goal configuration (right), the one shown here being used throughout the present experiment.
Thc Eight Puzzle is solved by dcriving information relevant to choosing moves from a comparison of the current puzzle configuration (PC) with thc goal configuration (GC).
PC and GC can be represented internally and compared with cach other in many ways.
For cxample, the subject can measure or estimate the qualitative similarity of PC to GC, or a numcerical "distance" of the one from the othcr.
Most artificial intelligence programs for solving the Fight Puzzle use some kind of distance mcasure that takes into account considcrable information about PC (Nilsson, 1971; Pohl, 1969).
On thc othcr hand, a program along the lines of the Gcncral Problem Solver (Newell, Shaw, & Siınon, 1958), would considcr the "major difference" (i.c., a feature like a particular tile not in its final position) between PC and GC, and would ignore most of the other information about PC.
These two general approaches make quitc different prcdictions about what we might expect to find in subjects' protocols.
The protocols of the subjects wcre categorized on the basis of mainly syntactic informnation (Ericsson, 1975b).Two categories, intentions and cognitions, have major relevance to the form of representation the subjects were using.
Intentions are verbalized goals, defining the attributes of configurations subjccts are secking to achieve (c.g., "I want to gct 3 in its correct placc").
Cognitions are verbalizcd characterizations of the current PC (c.g., "I see that 7 is in its correct place").
We will present our analysis of these two categories separately, a proccdure that will permit us to cvaluate, or at least comment on, the gencrality of the representation.
Our analysis cınploys 274 protocol segments coded as intentions, and 132 encoded as cognitions, pooled from the protocols of ten subjects.
We start by discussing intentions.
'The most striking finding about intentions is that subjects define goals in terms of only a few tiles (or one).
In 162 cases (59%) the goal involved positioning a singlc tile; a pair of tiles in 61 cases (22%).
Propcrties of three tiles were mentioned in 49 cases (18%), four tiles in two cases (1%).
In no case did a subject mention a goal of positioning more than four tiles.
'The majority (75%) of intentions involving single tiles expressed the goal of putting them in their "correct" position in the GC.
Somc examples of such verbalizations are given in 'Table 7-1.
Thesc arc exactly the kinds of goals that a GPS-like modcl would predict.
In the remaining cascs, subjccts vcrbalized "getting the tile closer to its goal" or "getting tile in its correct row," or "getting the tile to a location different from that in GC." or "getting rid of a blocking tile." Verbalized intentions involving two tiles are of two kinds (Ericsson, 1975b, discusses five cxceptions).
'The tiles are cither to bc placed in their correct positions, or in correct sequential order independently of absolute location.
It might be thought that these goals would involve all pairs of tiles adjacent in the GC.
In actual fact, with one exception, all such goals involvcd pairs of tiles with adjacent ordinal numbers (c.g., 1-2, 4-5, ctc.).
'This suggests an internal representation of the GC as shown in Figurc 7-2.
When we turn to intentions involving three or four tiles, thc same pattern cmcrges. Λll but five instances (47) involve the correct placement or correct sequential order of the tiles in the first or the second row of GC, that is, 1-2-3 or 4-5-6.

Of the 132 protocol segmcnts encoded as cognitions, 54 (41%) involved the attributes of a single tile, while 52 (39%) involved the attributes of a pair of tiles, and 18 (14%), threc tiles.

## Isomorphic
Problems Hayes and Simon (1974) proposed a model describing how subjects comprehend written problem instructions and construct an internal representation of problem information.
T’he model was able to gencrate problem representations for the Tea Ceremony problem, a formal isomorph of the 'Tower of Hanoi.
'Thinking-aloud protocols were gathcred from subjects presentcd with this problem, but the protocols proved to bc rather sketchy for the interval during which subjccts wcrc formulating the problem and devising a representation of it.
It was difficult, from these protocols, to determine what representations subjects had constructed.
However, as we shall see, protocols taken during the interval when subjects were solving the probleın disclosed these representations clearly.
In a subsequent study, Simon and Hayes (1976) uscd problem isomorphs that, their model predicted, would causc subjccts to adopt distinctly different problem representations.
Wc will consider here two of these isomorphs, a move problem and a change problem, respectively.
In its usual form, thc 'Tower of Hanoi involves moving of transferring disks among three pcgs.
Only onc disk can bc movcd at a time, and a larger disk cannot bc placcd on a peg on which therc is alrcady a smaller disk.
In this form, the 'Γower of Hanoi is a move problem.
The starting and goal configurations of disks and pegs are shown in Figure 7-3.
Herc thc pcgs arc labclcd "Λ, B, C" and thc disks are labcled "1 =small," "2= medium," "3= large," and will be rcferred to by these names in all the isomorphic problems.
Figure 7-3 Illustration of Different Representations in the Tower of Hanoi Problem with 3 Disks In the 'Tower of Hanoi, the disks retain thcir physical identities; only their locations (the pcgs on which they arc placcd) changc.
Symbolically, we can describe any disk configuration as a list of thrce locations (corresponding to the thrce pegs), and lists of the appropriate disks associated with cach location, (as shown in Figurc 7-3).
We will call this symbolic representation a move representation.
Alternatively, wc could rcprcsent cxactly the samc information synıbolically by a list of the three disks, and with cach member of the list, an indication of the pcg with which it is associated.
Wc will call this a change representation.
When a move representation is uscd, then an alteration in the problem situation is recorded by removing the name of one of the disks from its pcg list and placing it on the list of a differcnt pcg.
When a change representation is used, then an alteration in the problein situation is recorded by altering the name of the peg with which some particular disk is associated.
'Thus, the same move in the 'Towcr of Hanoi is represented by different symbol-manipulating processes in the two different symbolic representations of the task.
(See Figure 7-4.) Isomorphs of the Tower of Hanoi can be constructed by substituting other kinds of objects for disks and pegs, and the legal transformations with these objects can be described in terms of moves or changes.
Below, we give examples of problems in which the objects are "monsters" and "globes," and the transformations involve cither moving a globe from one monster to another, or changing the size of the globe.
Since these two problem descriptions are logically cquivalent (that is, isomorphic with respect to states and moves), it is logically possible that a subject would use either the change or move representation when faced with either of the problems.
The UNlERSTANI) model of Simon and Hayes (1976) made cxplicit predictions as to whcther subjects would represcnt particular problem statements as move or change problems.
In particular, it predicted for the examples presented here that the first would be represented as a move problem, and the second as a change problem.
'That is to say, if the problems were described to subjects as involving an object moving from one location to another, the subjects would represent it symbolically in just that way; while if it were dcscribed to them in terms of objects changing thcir sizcs or other propcrties, the subjects would represent it symbolically in that other way.
To provide evidence of the representations that the subjects used, two different kinds of protocol statcmcnts were analyzed for subjects presented with thesc problem isomorphs.
The statemcnts of the first kind were verbalized descriptions of moves, statcments of the second kind were verbalized descriptions of current problem states and configurations.

## 328
Protocol Analysis Three five-handed extraterrestial monsters were holding three crystal globes.
Because of the quantum-mechanical peculiarities of their neighborhood, both monsters and globes come in exactly three sizes with no others permitted: small, medium, and large.
The medium-sized monster was holding the small globe, the small monster was holding the large globe, and the large monster was holding the medium-sized globe.
Since this situation offended their keenly developed sense of symmetry, they proceeded to transfer globes from one monster to another so that each monster would have a globe proportionate to his own size.
Monster etiquette complicated the solution of the problem since it requires: 1. that only onc globe may be transferred at a time; 2. that if a monsier is holding two globes, only the larger of the two may be transferred; and 3. that a globe may not be transferred to a monster who is holding a larger globe.
By what sequence of transfers could the monsters have solved this problem?

## Strategies
for the Tower of Hanoi How can we predict verbalizations of subjects using different strategics to solve thc same problem?
In particular, can the stratcgics be identified reliably from protocols?
'lhe data are derived from a study by Neves (1977), in which he traincd subjects to use different strategies to solve the Tower of Hanoi puzzle, and then asked them to think aloud during the solution process.
First, we will summarizc the theorctical analysis of Simon (1975), describing several different strategies that all lcad to correct solutions of the puzzle.
'l’he analysis makes cxplicit what information enters and is retaincd in Sl'M at all times.
From the theoretical models we derive the sequence of hecded information for a numnber of puzzle configurations, and use these to predict what information would be verbalizcd with cach strategy.
We then encode protocols from subjects trained in using these stratcgies, and match them against the predictions.
The Tower of Hanoi puzzle has already been described carlier.
We will be concerncd with the 4-disk version.
At the start of thc probolem, the disks are all on Peg 1; the task is to move them to Peg 3.
Task Analysis.
'The theorctical models of the solution process are expressed in the form of production systems.
'T’his formalism is described by Simon (1975, pp.
274-275) as follows: Λ production system (Newell & Simon, 1972) is simply an ordered sct of processes called productions.
Fach production has two parts: a condition (C), and an action (∆), which are usually written with an arrow connccting them: C→ Λ.
'The reader will not mislead himself badly if he cquates the arrow in a production with the link in a spccial kind of S-R structure.
The productions fall into two classes: a general class and a special class called perceptual tests.
'l’he condition of a production belonging to the general class is a test usually for the prescnce of absencc of a particular kind of symbol on the contents of STM.
'The test is cither satisfied or not.
Whenever the test in thc condition part of a gencral production is satisficd, and only them, the action part is executed.
The action may be a motor act, the performing of a perceptual test, an act of retrieving information from long-term memory, or an act of changing the contents of short-tern memory.
'The condition part of a production ınay involve a conjunction of several clementary tests, and the action part may involve a sequence of elementary actions. Λ simple example of a general production is: # "Problem-solved" → Halt The condition side of this production calls for a test whcther the symbol, "Problem-solved," has been stored in S'IM.
The action taken in this case is to halt the cntire process.
1f the symbol is not found in STM, no action is taken.
'T’he production subsystem represcnting perceptual tests is activated by exccuting a 'Test action in one of the gencral productions.
The condition of a perccptual test is a perccivable feature of thc task environment, or a conjunction of such features.
If the fcature or conjunction of features is present, and only then, the action part of the perceptual test is executed.
T’he only action of a perceptual test is to change the contents of S'l'M.
Exccution of a perceptual test makes the systcm "aware" of some perceivable feature of its environment by storing information about that feature in SIM.
The production system and the perccptual subsystem arc cach assumed to operate serially only one production may be activated at a time.
If the conditions for more than one production are satisfied simultancously, only the first of these on the list of productions is activated.
Hence, the order of productions on the list is an integral part of the definition of thc program; changing the order could (and usually will) cause significant changes in the system's bchavior.
The advantages of production systems as programming formalisms, and the rcasons for thinking that strategics stored in the human central nervous system may be organized as production systems are discussed in Newell and Simon (1972, pp.
803-806), and in Newcll (1973).
'Thc particular kind of production system we are using here has two advantages worth mentioning.
First, it makes cxplicit exactly what information is held in short-term memory, so that processing assumptions that would place unrcalistic demands on SI'M are immcdiately detectable.
Second, the system makes cqually cxplicit what assumptions arc bcing made about perccptual capabilitics.
Features of the cnvironmcnt can only be taken into account by means of specific perceptual tests, and these tests can lead directly only to knowledge, not to action.
Simon (1975) describes a number of different stratcgies, among which we will consider here only the goal-recursive strategy.
The movepattern strategy is so different from these that it can be trivially distinguished from the other two with protocol data (Neves, 1977).
The goal-recursive strategy applies recursivcly a proccdure that allows the correct move to be gencrated for any configuration of the disks on the pegs.
Basic to the procedure is the concept of a pyramid of K disks (i.e., the pyramid consisting of all disks of size K and smaller).
The goal of moving Pyramid (K) to a given pcg can be attaincd by recursive application of the following proccdure: Try to move disk K to Peg (X): If such a move has already been made, crcate the goal of moving Pyramid (K—1) to Pcg (X).
If such a move can legally be made, make it.
If such a move cannot be made, create the goal of moving Pyramid (K—-1) to thc Other pcg (i.c., the peg that is ncither X nor the one on which disk K stands).
'lo scc why this stratcgy works, considcr an cxample.
First, if all the disks are in the starting position, the strategy first generates the goal of moving the pyramid of four disks to the goal peg.
Sincc the largest disk cannot lcgally be moved, the goal is gencrated of moving all the remaining disks to the other pcg.
Since thc largest of these remaining disks (Disk 3) also cannot be moved, thc goal is generated of moving the pyramid of the two smallest disks to the goal peg.
'This also fails, so the goal is now created of moving the smallest disk to the other pcg.
'This move is madc successfully.
Thc goal-recursive strategy is sufficicntly powerful to gencrate the correct move in any configuration of disks on the pcgs.

## Mental
Multiplication 'T'here are several rcasons why mental multiplication of two-digit numbers is an attractive task for intensive analysis.
Earlier work (lDansereau, 1969; l)anscrcau & Grcgg, 1967; Hitch, 1978) havc shown that subjects display a very orderly scquence of cognitive processes in this task.
'This orderliness allows us to make very strong predictions about the order in which information is heeded, and hencc, verbalized.
In the Appendix, we will argue that this kind of task is particularly useful for warming up subjects.
We can use it to calibratc the subjects' verbalization processes, and use this calibration in analyzing individual differences in performing less stercotyped tasks.
'T'he models we shall examine are aimed simply at identifying the information the subject needs in finding the intermcdiate and final results of the multiplication.
'They leave open more fundamcntal issues of how the numbers arc represented by the subject.
'The multiplication may be segmented into three major parts, to make the description casier to follow.

## PROCESSES
WITH ALTERNATIVE REALIZATIONS ln many cognitive tasks, the cxact verbalizations of a subjcct arc not detcrmincd uniqucly by the task, or even by the subject's stratcgy.
Under such circumstances, assessing whether a protocol fits the predictions of a model is a little like judging whether a sentcncc is grammatical.
Linguistics has traditionally relied on native informants for making judgmcnts of grammaticality.
Only very rccently has it been possible to attempt such assessments automatically with the aid of computers.
In the same way, most analyses of protocol data are carried out by investigators who have had cxtensive experiencc with the cognitive processes and their verbalization for the task under study.
Comparing a verbal protocol with the predictions of an informnation processing model involves a judgment not dissimilar to the judgment of grammaticality.
Its validity depends at lcast partly on the consensus of the judges.
'There are also some structural similarities betwcen utterances and cognitive processes that are worth noting.
It is not uncommon for people to start to say something and then to stop and begin a new sentence that is completed.
People also stop midway in sentences, and then restart by repeating some words and then completing the sentencc.
Similar interruptions and restarts occur in cognitive processes like those wc have already examined in this chapter, especially processes like mental multiplication and addition that gradually cumulate information.
In verbal reports, such interruptions or repetitions arc marked by intonation or explicit comment.
As far as possible, such occurrences should be identified when the verbal transcript is being preprocessed.

of Digits Returning to the addition task that was considcred in an carlicr section, we now go beyond the original analysis, which was limited to reports of intermediate inputs and results, and undcrtakc a morc complete examination of the full protocols.
We shall see how this additional information can be used to constrain the possible modcls of thc cognitive process.
Here are two protocols from the addition task: Formal task analysis.
M digits can be addcd together in many ways that form partial sums, and at last the final sum.
At the most general level, the task can be described by a sequcnce of internal states, each containing the set of digits not yet addcd and the partial sum just computcd.
'l'he initial state would be the sct of digits to be addcd, and the final state the sum of the whole set of digits.
'Thc scqucnce of partial sums will bc defincd uniqucly if cach contains all the digits already summed.
However, a subjcct might rctain scveral partial sums for subsets of digits, these to be added together subsequently.
'The formal task analysis does not provide more than hints as to how thc subject might represent the task information internally.
'There arc two kinds of information the subject nceds to know at all times: (1) which digits have not yet been proccsscd (the digits are available in a visually accessiblc row), and (2) the partial sums that have not yet been incorporated in the total.
Each partial sum can be represented by a onc- or two-digit number.
Wc know that normal subjects, without extensive practice, can retain only a few numbers in memory.
Partial sums are particularly difficult to rctain, for they arc modified and changed frequently.
From studies of short-term memory, Waugh and Norman (1965) showed that only 4 digits could be kept readily accessible in short-term meımory while a task was being performed.
From these findings we would predict that subjects will use only a sımall number of different partial sums (probably onc, or possibly two) when they are trying to add sets of digits rapidly.
Assume that the subject remembers the digits to be added in terms of their location on the stimulus card.
After more than four or five digits have been proccssed and added, a non-trivial amount of information is needed to keep track of the processed and unprocessed digits.
How much information is necded depends on the order in which the digits are cumulated.
Consider a random ordering, and an ordering from left to right, respectively (T’here is an X below cach processed digit.): <table><tr><td colspan="10">Random case:</td></tr><tr><td>3</td><td>0 8 X</td><td>1</td><td>2 X</td><td>4</td><td>9 X</td><td>0</td><td>6</td><td>7 X</td><td>3 X</td></tr><tr><td colspan="10">Preferred case:</td></tr><tr><td>3</td><td>0 8</td><td>1</td><td>2</td><td>4</td><td>9</td><td>0</td><td>6</td><td>7</td><td>3</td></tr><tr><td>X</td><td>X</td><td>X X</td><td></td><td></td><td></td><td></td><td></td><td></td><td></td></tr></table> In the random case, the identities of the five processed digits or the six unprocessed digits have to bc remembercd, a substantial memory load.
In the ordered case, the subject need only kecp note of the last processed digit, or the one to be processed next.
After a digit has been processed, attention moves to the one immediately to its right.
We can usc this large difference in ST'M rcquiremcnts, together with our knowledge of the capacity of STM, to predict that subjects will, in fact process the digits in scquential order and not in random order.
Following Newell and Simon (1972), a similar argument can be made that limits on the processes available are the principal constraints on the processing strategy that will be used.

Advantages of Local Fncoding.
Wc havc now outlined a spacc of possiblc verbalizations of cognitive processes in thc addition task, and havc analyzed the SI'M limits on the stratcgies availablc to subjects in pcrforming the task.
We have shown how protocols can be cncoded to reveal the steps taken and the informnation heeded.
From these encodings, we can draw many inferences about the organization and structure of the cognitive processes for solving the complete problems.
This "bottom up" approach to cncoding, in which cach verbalization is encodcd ncarly indcpendcntly of its context, scems to us to have advantages, where it is feasible, over more global approaches.
We wish to consider these advantages in a little more detail.
In Chapter 6, we discussed at somc length how to cvaluate the evidential support for a given description of a protocol.
A human encoder who uses a global approach will arguc that thc mcchanisms postulated in his description are plausible, and will hope that other investigators will find his account persuasivc.
One kind of argument that is frequently used is to show that the proposed interpretation satisfies the constraints that are known to apply to the human information processing systcm.
Additional empirical support for an interpretation can be derived from a local encoding approach.
'The strength of local encoding is that cach scgment is encoded independently (or ncarly indcpendently) of context.
If the pattern of cach, or many, scgments can be predicted from a model, cach scgmcnt provides an indepcndent data point for the model.
Consider, by way of examplc, the following protocol:

Error analysis.
In our carlicr analysis of thc arithmctic task, we suggested that three types of errors are particularly likely to occur.
'The first two have to do with the gencration and retention of intermcdiate results.
The last has to do with kecping track of the digits not yct added.

Inferring process models.
A number of issucs arise in using protocol data to infer process models.
We will considcr three of them here: First, what gencralizable infcrences can be drawn from protocols; Second, how can the stability and instability of cognitive proccsses be studied using protocols; 'Third, what can we learn from retrospective reports about the addition task?
The information reported by subjects in the addition task consists almost exclusively of intermediate sums and stimulus digits.
One may conclude from the absence of other information that selection rules to choose the next digits for addition and other strategic rules in the performancc strategy arc highly "automated" and governcd in considerable part by recognition processes.
'There may, of course, be some differences in these processes from one subject to another.
Insofar as they lead to different orderings of the processes, hencc to different sequences of digits, they can be inferred from the protocols.
Examination of a large number of protocols enables us to define the space of possible strategies, and to arrive at conclusions about which stratcgics are common, and which ones rare in the population of subjects.
Buswcll (1928) cites many intcresting cxamples of deviant rules for adding and subtracting numbers, inferred from studies of school children.

## RELIABILITY
OF VERBAL REPORTS The reproducibility of data on repcated test occasions is critical to its interpretation.
An obvious approach to showing rcproducibility is to give the same subjccts thc same tasks on scveral occasions, and then compare the verbal reports.
In Chapter 3, wc have alrcady discussed the complex issucs involved in reproducing cognitive processes cxperimentally.
Systematic differences might arise from one reproduction to the next because of specific memory for the previous solution to the task, gradually acquired skill in the task, and generalizcd learning of skills applicable to the task domain.
Even in a single session, cognitive processes in the same task may show considerable variation.
'Thus it is hard to produce identity in cognitive processes on two successive occasions.
In one particular kind of situation we are assured that successive verbal reports reflect, accurately or not, the same cognitive process.
'This is when we obtain concurrent and retrospective reports from the same subject for the same task performance.
In Chapter 5, we discussed some general differences between concurrent and retrospective reports that are predicted by our model.
'The retrospective report may, in particular, be expected to be less complete than the concurrent onc, but they should agrcc on the information they both contain. ln this section, we will review some evidence for this prediction of consistency.
There are only a few studies of the reliability and consistency of verbal reports.
We will review most of thc studics wc arc acquainted with together with some of our own data.
We will organize our presentation around scvcral studies that have addresscd both thc issucs of reliability and consistency.
Our discussion will make cxtensive use of individual protocols, to give the reader some fecling for the kinds of behavior that may be encountered.
Because of thc limited availability of data, we will draw only very tentative gencralizations from them.

On the final occasion, the subjcct gencrated the correct solution directly.
Hagert built a computer model, in the form of a production system, that prcdicted quite accurately the information in 98% of the protocol segments from the first occasion.
However, the model could account for less than half of the fragments from the other two protocols.
But with local and minor changes, the model could account for up to 90% of the scgments in these protocols.
'T'he protocol from the second occasion could be described accurately if two processing crrors were allowed when premises involving "right of' or "left of' were converted into sequential ordcrings.
Modifying a single rule involved in chccking the corrcctness of the tentative orderings improved the description of the third protocol.
Although these modifications werc post hoc changes, with the bencfit of hindsight, still the analysis indicates that the subjcct's cognitive processes remained substantially the same at a stratcgic lcvel through three problem-solving sessions extending over two years.

## Λ Memory
Task Ericsson and Polson (in preparation) studied a waiter who could memorize dinner orders from more than 16 pcople without cxternal memory aids.
When we are looking at a highly skilled and rapid performance of this kind, we would expect high rcliability in the content and structure of the cognitive processing.
Ericsson and Polson created an expcrimcntal analoguc to the restaurant situation by selecting a subset of itcms (8 differcnt stcaks, 5 durations of cooking, 5 salad dressings, and 3 different starches). Λ computer gencrated a random combination of these items for simulated diners (represented by photographs).
'I’he experimenter read the complete order (4 items) as the subject (the expert waiter) pointed to the corresponding face.
'T'he subject was encouraged to take all the orders as rapidly as possible without making crrors in the subscquent recall.
'The waiter did not recall the orders as presented, but instead recalled them by category, that is, first all the salad dressings, then the steaks, etc.
For items within a category, he formed groups or chunks of four items.
'To remember these items, he relicd on various mnemonic encodings, for example, remembering the first letter for salad dressings.
The four letters for the dressings could often be recoded as an English word.

As expected, the two concurrent protocols arc remarkably similar.
The differences relate to very local processes and not to the basic structure of the skill.
'The retrospective reports resemble cach other as closely or more closely than they do the corresponding concurrent protocols.
The protocol study, while only a single example of verbalized data from highly skilled performance, should demonstrate the fcasibility of cxamining the stability and adaptation of processes under varying conditions.
There have been similar findings of reliability in othcr rescarch on mnemonic encodings (Chase and Ericsson, 1981, 1982) and medical diagnosis (Wortman, 1966).

## Summary
The comparisons of concurrent and retrospcctive reports in this chapter and Chaptcr 5 are in substantial agrecment in showing that thc reports arc mutually consistent, the rctrospective reports often omitting information contained in the concurrent reports.
Comparison of thinkingaloud protocols for the same task on successive occasions shows greater variability.
For somc highly practiced skills, like mental addition and the memorization of our skilled waiter, thcre is rcmarkable consistency from one occasion to another.
In the case of protocols where subjects had only a little experience with thc task, therc is littlc cvidencc that subjects reused specific information from a previous solution or acquired gencralized knowledge or skill for the task domain (Hagert's subject on the third occasion may bc a partial exccption to this last claim).
'Ihe variability observed in thc protocols may be vicwed as "local" (low-level) variability in the cognitive processes.
Morc important than the fact that there is somc variability is the cqually prominent fact that there is grcat stability of the successive protocols in terms of strategies and representations.
