## CONCLUDING
REMARKS AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS In thc beginning of this book we proposcd that cognitive processes could be describcd as sequences of heeded information and cognitive structures and that yerbal reports correspondcd to this hecded information.
The examples discussed in this chapter illustrate how verbalizations can be encoded and matched against hypotheses about the structure and sequcnce of the hecded information.
T’he rather extensive literature using protocols as data has, for the most part, relicd on methods and encoding schemes that are similar to those described here, which we view mainly as extensions and explications of previous studies.
In the beginning of this book we argucd that verbal reports should be scen as onc of many sources of data about cognitive processes and structures, and that modcls and mcthods accounting for verbal data should not bc different, in principle, from accounts of other types of data.
It is essential that the mcthodology for using verbal reports be wholly integrated with the main strcam of experimental psychology and other arcas of cognitive science.
Many of the most recent studies have quite successfully cmbedded the collection of verbal reports within expcrimcntal designs and have addressed issucs of generalizability.
However, we need many more studics of this kind to provide models for verbal reports analysis.
Considerable progress has also been made toward integrating the morc detailed analyses and models of verbal reports with existing theories and models.
Maybe the greatest challenge is presented by the mathcmatical models of performance of groups of subjects.
We need to be able to identify the structural and process characteristics that give rise to thesc confirmed regularitics of performancc.
In Chapter 4 we made a first attempt to show how such a mapping can bc carried out between gencral characteristics of heeded information and regularities of performance.
We also want to point to Einhorn, Klcinmuntz, and Kleinmuntz's (1979) analysis showing the consistcncy bctween process models derived from verbal reports and the more traditional mathematical regression models.
However, much more thcorctical and analytical work is required to achieve a complete integration of these different bodics of data and theory.
In thc beginning of Psychology, many influcntial psychologists vicwed verbal reports, and more preciscly introspection, as the only valid method for data-collection in psychology.
At a later period, during the reign of behaviorism, verbal reports were almost totally rejected as data.
It is now time for verbal reports to reassume their position as a rich source of data, combinable with other data, that can be of the greatest value in providing an integrated and full account of cognitive processes and structures.
In this appendix we will give some practical advicc and information on how to clicit various types of verbal reports under standard conditions.
Tasks and situations that require variations of the standard procedure are discussed in Chapter 5.
We will distinguish three types of verbal reports, namcly talk-aloud, think-aloud and retrospective reports.
Apart from discussing the verbal reports individually we will also describe the recommended procedure, wherc both think-aloud and retrospective reports are clicited for the same process.
We should point out that the suggestions expressed herc are based on our experiencc and intuitions, rather than experimental studies.
We hopc such systcmatic studies will be made in the future.
First, we will briefly comment on some variables relating to the experimcntal situation, then we will describe instructions and warm up procedures for the two different types of verbalizing procedures.
In many studics we want to collect verbal reports for cognitive processes that are no different from those occurring in traditional cxperiments.
Apart from the instruction to verbalize and the production of the verbalization, the only differences are the presence of thc monitoring expcrimenters and of the tape recorder.
After a short timc subjects become accustomed to both the experimentcr and tape-recorder.
In many tasks, espccially problem-solving tasks, subjects get so involved in the task that little noticc is taken of the environment, and situational factors have no real cffect.
For other cases, wc have found it better to keep the tapc-rccorder and the experimenter outside the view of the subject.
Most high quality tapc-rccorders are able to adapt their sensitivity automatically and thus give good rccording quality cven when placed slightly bchind the subject.
'The cxpcrimenter can also be scated bchind the subjcct.
Evidencc from verbalization of free associations in clinical situations suggest that it is bctter to have the analyst outside thc view of the subjcct, like bchind the coach (Havens, 1973: Frcud, 1963, pp.
135-156).
If rcmindcrs, like "kccp talking", are used, the subjcct will not feel obliged to address the experimenter or turn around to answer him.
The number of verbalizations that are social and directcd to the cxperimenter may be uscd to evaluate how much the expcrimenter has intruded (cf.
Ohlsson, 1980).

## TALK-ALOUD
When wc arc interested in prescrving thc tcmporal propertics of the cognitive process we may ask our subjects to talk aloud.
Of course, it is only for tasks where we can assumnc subjccts rcly on oral codes that we can expcct to gct much verbalization with such an instruction.
The proccdure we use contains a gencral instruction and a couple of warm-up tasks.
'The warm-up tasks are sclcctcd to bc particularly easy to use "talk-aloud" with and onc's for which the cognitive proccsscs are well understood.
Here is a sample instruction for talk-aloud.

## INSTRUCTION:
In this experiment we are interested in what you say to yourself as you perform some tasks that we give you. in order to do this we will ask you to TALK ALOUD as you work on the problems.
What l mean by talk aloud is that I want you to say out loud everything that you say to yourself silently.
Just act as if you are alone in the room speaking to yourself.
If you are silent for any length of time I will remind you to keep talking aloud.
Do you understand what I want you to do?
Good, before we turn to the real experiment, we will start with a couple of practice problems.
I want you to talk aloud while you do these problems.
First, I will ask you to multiply two numbers in your head.
So talk aloud while you multiply 24 times 34!

## Good!
Now I would like you to solve an anagram.
I will show you a card with scrambled letters.
It is your task to find an English word that consists of all the presented letters.
For example, if the scrambled letters are KORO, you may see ihat these letters spell the word ROOK.
Any questions?
Please "talk aloud" while you solve the following anagram! <NPEPHA = HAPPEN> Good!
These warm-up cxercises have several purposes.
First, we want subjects to begin talk aloud under circumstances where it is comparatively casy.
Sccond, we want to make ccrtain that all subjccts talk aloud.
If particular subjects appear not to verbalize as much as normal subjects, one can give them more practice problems.
Furthermore, one can ask them for a retrospective report after they complete the task.
Either the subjcct will notice the discrepancy bctween talk-aloud protocol and retrospection, or the experimenter will see that the subject did talk aloud.
In our experience it is very rarc that subjects do not spontancously verbalize in a normal fashion after a couple of practice problems.
It also happens that subjects occasionally "think aloud" rather than "talk aloud".
In this case subjects will verbally describe thc spatial arrangement of numbers in a mental multiplication and refer to them by their spatial location.
Subjects can then be asked to do the corresponding task silently to realize that they takc much longer whilc verbalizing, or the experimenter can ask "I)id you say X to yourself silently?" Simply recording the time often leads subjects to the more rapid "talk aloud".
Selecting tasks for warm-up exercises is not casy.
Somctimes mental multiplications are too difficult and embarrass the subject.
For such subjccts mental addition of 2- or 3-digit numbers may bc more appropriate.
Other possible tasks are, "Find as many words as possible that rhyme with 'beef," "Gcnerate as many words as possible using the letters like 'ONDTERH!'."

## THINK-ALOUD
WITH RETROSPECTIVE REPORTS Rather than considcring think-aloud and retrospective reports separately, we will discuss them as parts of a more gencral procedure, which we recommend be used whether think-aloud or retrospective reports or both be given for the same cognitive proccss.
'The main reason for combining them in a common warm-up proccdure is that for cognitive processes of intermcdiate duration we cxpcct the "think aloud" protocol and the retrospective report to contain basically the same information.
Hence by having the subject give both reports for the same cognitive process we are in a position to assess completeness of the think-aloud protocol and assure that the retrospective rcport contains an actual record of the cognitivc process. Λ general instruction with warm-up cxamples is given bclow.
In this experiment we are interested in what you think about when you find answers to some questions that I am going to ask you to answer.
In order to do this l am going to ask you to THINK ALOUD as you work on the problem given.
What I mean by think aloud is that I want you to tell me EVERYTHING vou are thinking from the time you first see the question until you give an answer.
I would like you to talk aloud CONSTANTLY from the time I present each problem until you have given your final answer to the question.
I don't want you to try to plan out what you say or try to explain to me what you are saying.
Just act as if you are alone in the room speaking to yourself.
It is most important that you keep talking.
If you are silent for any long period of time I will ask you to talk.
Do you undersland what l want you to do?
Good, now we will begin with some practice problems.
First, I want you to multiply these two numbers in your head and tell me what you are thinking as you get an answer.
"What is the result of multiplying 24 x 36" Good, now I want to see how much you can remember about what you were thinking from the time you read the question until you gave the answer.
We are interested in what you actually can REMEMBER rather than what you think you must have thought.
If possible I would like you to tell about your memories in the sequence in which they occurred while working on the question.
Please tell me if you are uncertain about any of your memories.
I don't want you to work on solving the problm again, just report all that you can remember thinking about when answering the question.
Now tell me what you remember.
Good.
Now I will give you two more practice problems before we proceed with the main experiment.
I want you to do the same thing for each of these problems.
I want you to think aloud as before as you think about the question, and after you have answered it I will ask you to report all that you can remember about your thinking.
Any questions?
Here is your next problem.
"How many windows are there in your parent's house?" Now tell me all that you can remember about your thinking.
Good, now here is another practice problem.
Please think aloud as you try to answer it.
There is no need to keep count, I will keep track for you.
"Name 20 animals".
Now tell me all that you can remember about your thinking.
This warm-up proccdure is bascd on the observation that it helps subjects verbalize oral information concurrently.
Morc importantly, the easy and dircct verbalization of such information makes it clcar to the subject that think-aloud involves concurrent verbalization of heeded thoughts rather a retrospectivc and cxplanatory report, which subjects may be more familiar with.
Hence, the first task, or morc if that is required, is the same as used to clicit talk-aloud verbalization.
'The only differcnce is that with think-aloud instruction wc admit or even encourage verbalization of information that was cncoded in non-verbal form.
The over-all idea is to present the subject with warm-up tasks until he or she is comfortable in thinking aloud and provides reports of the same information in both rctrospective and concurrent reports.
Occasionally the cxpcrimenter may be rcquired to point out differences bctween information reported during think-aloud and retrospectively reported information.
Also, subjects may use a more retrospective mode of reporting during think-aloud, or during the retrospective report engage in analysis of why they thought in a certain way, cspecially if they recognize making errors.
(For a more detailed discussion of deviation from think-aloud and retrospective report, sec Chapter 5, 6, and 7).
Most of these deviations can be sct straight by simply repcating key phrases of the gencral instruction.
Some subjects may be bencfitted by interspersing silent trials, for which the solution time is recordcd, to assure that they are not changing their mode of thought to accomodate verbalization.
During the actual expcriment we rccommend that both think-aloud and retrospective reports be recorded.
Even for cognitive processes of long duration, where we know that thc retrospcctive report will be incomplcte, it will be quite useful.
In this case, it will more clcarly convey the gencral structure of the process, as most of the detailed information will not be retricved, and retricval will use the higher-level organizational cues, like subgoals, or recall cues.

See also Levcl l verbalization Verbalization processes, specification of, 224-25; taxonomy of, 12 Verbalized rules, and behavior, 24-25, 137-39 Verbalizing, cognitive processes, 243-45; with multiple stimuli, 74-75 Verbosity, 21 Verbalizing procedures, types of, 15-24 Verbs as cucs, 223 Veridical content, 33 Veridicality of verbalizations, 109 Visual encodings, verbalization of, 95-100 Visual stimuli, oral rccoding of, 67; vocalization of, 70.
See also I cvel 2 verbalization Vocalization, 15-16; of presented stimuli, 70-71; suppression of, 64; time requirements for, 67-68 Vocalize proccss, 227 Voting behavior, prediction of, 48 Warm-up tasks, 240-41, 257, 342, 355 Wuerzburg psychologists, 54 "Although the theory of verbal reports is psychologically interesting in and of itself, this book will undoubtedly be read for its more practical aspects, as well.
It provides an excellent introduction for those who wish to learn protocol analysis and a valuable reference for those who use it.
Ericsson and Simon give a detailed discussion of how to code and analyze protocols, including a significant number of worthwhile examples.
It is very fitting that one of the pioneers of the modern use of verbal data, Herb Simon, should be one of the authors of this important and sorely needed book." —MICHELENE T.
H.
CHI, University of Pittsburgh "This is an extremely important book.
The use of verbal reports as data has been important in a number of areas of cognitive psychology.
Protocol Analysis describes the strengths and weaknesses of the method and provides a conceptual framework within which to interprēt the data generated by it.
This is the kind of book that will become required reading for practitioners of cognitive science.” —GARY M.
OLSON, The University of Michigan “This book is extremely well written.
I believe it may persuade senior researchers in the field who have not used protocol analysis in the past to incorporate it in future work.
More important I believe it will be an effective device for educating young psychologists in this important methodology.
Thus, I would expect it to be useful both as a reference book and as a textbook." -BARBARA HAYES-ROTH, Stanford University
